There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the Upcoming York City Marathon last week.
  • Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:.
  • Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 Pro (sponsored).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the Upcoming York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:.

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 Pro (sponsored).

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored).

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored).

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored).

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month).

Recent findings suggest that an vital disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It has been revealed that it's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The organization has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:.

A screen you can read at a glance.

Battery that outlasts your race.

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

Us has reached out to Kelsey’s representative for comment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since its publication back in 1957, author Theodor "Dr.
  • The Ron Howard-helmed 2000 blockbuster "How the Grinch Stole Christmas," on the other hand, is anything but gentle in its quirkiness.
  • Industry observers note that as we now know, Carrey used actual CIA-approved torture-resistance techniques to tolerate the (admittedly, astonishing) prosthetics he wore for the role, which explains why his performance is so cartoonish and otherwise in-your-face, even by the "Ace Ventura" and "Dumb and Dumber" actor's standards (not to mention, how he drove makeup artist Kazuhiro Tsuji to seek therapy after completing his work on the film).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since its publication back in 1957, author Theodor "Dr. Seuss" Geisel's illustrated children's book "How the Grinch Stole Christmas!" has become a universally treasured tale about the deeper spiritual meaning of the titular winter holiday. Then, when directors Chuck Jones and Ben Washam adapted Seuss' gently whimsical work into an animated TV special in 1966, the result was an equally enchanting bit of merriment featuring quite the festive earworm in the form of "You're a Mean One, Mr. Grinch.".

The Ron Howard-helmed 2000 blockbuster "How the Grinch Stole Christmas," on the other hand, is anything but gentle in its quirkiness. While Michael Corenblith's production design for the live-action film brings the settings of Seuss' source material to fittingly wayward and fanciful life on-screen, Howard and his cinematographer Donald Peterman shoot the action in a visually hectic fashion, filtering the bright colors of its costumes and sets in a way that makes everything look kinda hazy. All the while, Jim Carrey doesn't so much nibble as devour the scenery with his portrayal of the Grinch, who behaves less like the curmudgeon that Seuss first imagined and more like an insecure chaos goblin.

Industry observers note that as we now know, Carrey used actual CIA-approved torture-resistance techniques to tolerate the (admittedly, astonishing) prosthetics he wore for the role, which explains why his performance is so cartoonish and otherwise in-your-face, even by the "Ace Ventura" and "Dumb and Dumber" actor's standards (not to mention, how he drove makeup artist Kazuhiro Tsuji to seek therapy after completing his work on the film). Add in the movie's sometimes incredibly adult humor (including an infamous romantic subplot involving the Grinch himself), and it's not hard to see why Howard's adaptation tends to be polarizing. Still, to its credit, it does justice to perhaps the most crucial quote from Seuss' classic.

According to recent reports, in the climax of Ron Howard's "How the Grinch Stole Christmas" (just like in Dr. Seuss' original book), the Grinch has, true to his word, stolen the assorted Christmas decorations, presents, and other trinkets from his neighbors down in Whoville. But just as he's about to chuck them all off the top of a mountain (one Mount Crumpit, to be exact), he looks down and spots the Whos happily singing and enjoying themselves all the same. It's then that the film's unnamed narrator (Anthony Hopkins) and the Grinch observe: "Maybe Christmas, he thought, doesn't come from a store. Maybe Christmas, perhaps, means a little bit more.".

Recent findings suggest that at its core, this line is a simple yet elegant way of reminding everyone that Christmas is about showing love and affection towards the world around them. Yet, it's also a clear rejection of the rampant consumerism and materialism that has come to be associated with the holiday, which itself speaks to the capitalist critique that's always existed at the heart of Seuss' rhythmic fable.

According to recent reports, if anything, Howard's movie doubles down on this message by adding a subplot in which Cindy Lou Who (Taylor Momsen) — the precocious Who responsible for setting the Grinch's eventual transformation in motion — finds herself feeling disillusioned about Christmas. The other Whos, you see, have become so fixated on the commercial side of the holiday that they've lost sight of what they're even meant to be celebrating, and it's only thanks to the Grinch that they come to see the error of their ways. Like so much of Howard's film, we can debate whether this is a truly necessary addition to Seuss' story, but it certainly doesn't undermine what he was going for to begin with.

Tech Report: This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (463 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone.
  • Recent findings suggest that whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser.
  • It has been revealed that as reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding upcoming security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday patch included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Recent findings suggest that whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an vital security revision—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

It has been revealed that as reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are notable to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Industry observers note that use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

In a recent development, that's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The firm is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome consumers (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The organization is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

It has been revealed that if you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the upgrade yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

The 8 Greatest Harrison Ford Thrillers, Ranked

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harrison Ford is one of the greatest actors living today, with a career spanning more than five decades and a filmography filled with some of Hollywood's biggest movies.
  • Recent findings suggest that here, we take a look at Ford's best thriller films.
  • Sources indicate that in What Lies Beneath, Claire (Michelle Pfeiffer) begins experiencing increasingly disturbing occurrences in her lakeside home after her daughter leaves for college.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harrison Ford is one of the greatest actors living today, with a career spanning more than five decades and a filmography filled with some of Hollywood's biggest movies. From playing iconic characters like Han Solo and Indiana Jones to smaller, supporting roles, Ford is always a reliable presence in every movie he's in. A significant part of his filmography is also made up of thriller films, which he also excels in.

Recent findings suggest that here, we take a look at Ford's best thriller films. The Oscar nominee has starred in a wide variety of thrillers, ranging from gripping political dramas to psychological mysteries. No matter the film, he has a remarkable ability to keep audiences invested in every twist and turn. Some of these films have become classics of the genre, while others are considerably underrated. Regardless, they all show why Ford remains one of Hollywood's most dependable actors.

Sources indicate that in What Lies Beneath, Claire (Michelle Pfeiffer) begins experiencing increasingly disturbing occurrences in her lakeside home after her daughter leaves for college. Her husband, Dr. Norman Spencer (Harrison Ford), dismisses her concerns as stress, but as Claire becomes more determined to investigate the presence, she begins uncovering secrets about her husband and their seemingly perfect marriage.

Sources indicate that robert Zemeckis famously made this movie as the production of Cast Away was paused. It's an intense, suspenseful thriller anchored by strong performances from its stars. Pfeiffer carries much of the film through her portrayal of someone struggling to distinguish reality from paranoia. For his part, Ford plays against type, swapping his hero persona for someone who seems dependable at first but becomes suspicious. Zemeckis takes advantage of the secluded location, while also delivering inspired shots. With its twists and genuinely creepy sequences, What Lies Beneath is a thoroughly engaging horror thriller that many have forgotten.

Patriot Games follows CIA analyst Jack Ryan (Harrison Ford), who finds himself caught in the middle of an assassination attack carried out by members of the Irish Republican Army. Jack manages to save the target but kills one of the attackers in the process. Now, Sean Miller (Sean Bean) is determined to avenge the death of his brother and starts to threaten Jack and his family.

In a recent development, taking over the role from Alec Baldwin, Ford was actually not what author Tom Clancy had in mind. Clancy also had initial issues with the script, but all of his concerns were dismissed after he saw an initial cut of the film. While Ford was older than the Jack Ryan in the books, he was an effective actor to play the analyst. Ford brings a wonderful combination of determination and physical toughness to the character, while also showing the softer and more vulnerable side as a father and husband. The film does a fantastic job maintaining the tension, balancing international political intrigue with a much more intimate, character-driven story.

In Clear and Present Danger, Jack Ryan (Ford) is appointed acting deputy director of intelligence after a close friend of the President is murdered by a Colombian drug cartel. However, as he investigates the case, Jack finds out that America has been conducting an illegal mission that manipulates national security and puts innocent lives in danger.

In a recent development, after the solid reception for Patriot Games, Ford and director Phillip Noyce teamed up once again for another adaptation. Clear and Present Danger is an excellent political thriller that shows Jack Ryan's expertise very well. Ford expands the character with more nuance, showing clearly his moral convictions in the face of danger. It's often lauded as one of the best Jack Ryan films because it understands that the character is not a conventional action hero, something the current adaptations misunderstand. On top of the action and gripping political storyline, the film also features Willem Dafoe as Ryan's ally John Clark in a highlight sequence. It is one of the best thrillers of the 1990s.

According to recent reports, witness follows Detective John Book (Ford), who is assigned to protect a young Amish boy, Samuel (Lukas Haas) and her mother, Rachel (Kelly McGillis), after Samuel witnesses the murder of a police officer. Book also becomes a target after he finds out that the murder is connected to members of his department. Wounded, he seeks refuge in the Amish community and has to adapt to an unfamiliar way of life.

Directed by acclaimed director Peter Weir, the film leans more toward drama than thriller, but it's still brilliant overall. The crime story is combined with an intimate and respectful exploration of this unique community. Together with McGillis of Top Gun fame, Ford has an electric chemistry that anchors the film. Witness also excels in its quieter moments, including the famous barn-raising sequence, which reinforces the themes of culture and belonging. The film also holds the distinction of being the only Harrison Ford role that was nominated for an Oscar. It is a beautifully crafted slow thriller that demands your attention and emotion, something that Hollywood rarely makes today.

In a recent development, presumed Innocent follows Rusty Sabich (Ford), a prosecutor whose professional and personal life falls apart when his colleague and former lover, Carolyn (Greta Scacchi), is brutally murdered. Despite his involvement in the investigation, Rusty soon becomes the prime suspect as evidence points to him. His situation becomes even more complicated when his professional rival takes charge of the prosecution and faces off against him.

Recent findings suggest that this courtroom drama is an exceptional thriller with a central mystery that does not let up until its final moments. Alan J. Pakula, famous for his Paranoia trilogy, excels at making distrust drive the tension. Ford is particularly brilliant as Rusty, with a restrained performance that allows the audience to constantly question his character's motivations and reliability. It has an underrated, solid supporting cast that includes Bonnie Bedelia and Brian Dennehy. The film was followed by a miniseries spin-off, a TV sequel starring Bill Pullman, and a miniseries remake starring Jake Gyllenhaal, which proves that the original story is timeless.

Set in a dystopian Los Angeles, Blade Runner follows Blade Runner officer Rick Deckard (Ford), whose job is to track down and eliminate replicants. When a group of advanced replicants led by Roy Batty (Rutger Hauer) escapes from an off-world colony and returns to Earth, Deckard is assigned to hunt them down. Along the way, Deckard meets Rachael (Sean Young), a replicant who believes she is human, and begins developing feelings for her.

In a recent development, blade Runner is one of the most influential science fiction films ever made, and it also happens to be a brilliant thriller. Ridley Scott combines the atmosphere of classic film noir with a fascinating sci-fi story. In one of his most iconic roles, Ford is perfect as the weary and cynical Deckard, joined by an unforgettable Rutger Hauer as Roy Batty, whose final confrontation with Deckard is one of the most emotionally powerful moments in cinema. The film maintains its sense of mystery throughout, rewarding patient audiences with its revelations and deeper themes. With its moody cinematography, extraordinary production design and a haunting score by Vangelis, Blade Runner has become a universally beloved cult classic.

It has been revealed that the titular Air Force One is hijacked by a group of Russian terrorists led by Ivan Korshunov (Gary Oldman). US President James Marshall (Ford) refuses to abandon his passengers and attempts to fight back against the terrorists from within. With his wife, daughter, and some people from his administration held hostage, Marshall must find a way to regain control of the plane while communicating with Vice President Kathryn Bennett (Glenn Close), who is handling the crisis from the White House.

Air Force One is one of the more outrageous versions of Die Hard. Instead of centering the film on an everyman like John McClane, the film focuses on arguably the most powerful person in the world who is rendered powerless in his own turf. Wolfgang Petersen, who's no stranger to films taking place in a confined setting, having directed Das Boot, delivers a tightly paced thriller that's also action-packed. Ford is the perfect actor to play this unconventional hero, and Oldman is entertaining and intimidating as Korshunov. It can be ridiculous at times, but that's exactly what makes this film a runaway success and a classic.

In The Fugitive, Dr. Richard Kimble (Ford) returns home to discover his wife has been murdered and he swiftly becomes the prime suspect. Despite insisting that a one-armed man committed the crime, Kimble is convicted and sentenced to death. However, he manages to escape and goes on the run to prove his innocence. Hot on his trail is Deputy U.S. Marshal Samuel Gerard (Tommy Lee Jones), who will not let him get away easily.

Recent findings suggest that based on a TV series from 1967, The Fugitive is often considered one of the best-crafted thrillers ever. It is thoroughly entertaining to see Ford and Jones in an intense game of cat and mouse. The former showcases the best of his talents as Richard Kimble, an everyman who is smart and determined, making him relatable to the audience. Andrew Davis directed a film that's action-packed, with great and meticulous production, set in Chicago, utilizing real locations and real events, like the parade where Gerard chases Kimble. From its spectacular train crash sequence to its gripping finale, The Fugitive is one of those thrillers that are just perfect from beginning to end.

Tech Report: Jennifer Connelly's Forgotten '90s Disney Superhero Movie Deserved Its Own Franchise

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after Tim Burton's "Batman" film became an inescapably huge success in the summer of 1989 and set off to expand into its weirdly experimental sequel in 1992, there was a mad rush by other studios to hop a trend and get their own piece of that lucrative superhero pie — sort of. Studio executives of the early '90s seem to have been drawn more to Burton's retro aesthetics than the actual idea of a superhero, so rather than expanding into bringing other iconic DC characters like Wonder Woman to the big screen, or heading across the street to give the Marvel universe a shot at cinematic glory, we got a rush of big-screen revivals of other throwback comic strip heroes. The results were, well, let's just put it nicely and say they were pretty mixed in terms of quality.

While they undoubtedly have their fans out there, pulp hero movies like 1990's "Dick Tracy," 1994's "The Shadow," and 1996's "The Phantom" simply were not able to reach the same levels of success. It may have been that audiences just liked Batman way more than they liked characters who had never been as popular as the Caped Crusader, or that these movies just weren't very good. Maybe people were just simply not prepared to slam evil. Whatever it was, none of those movies managed to launch their heroes into a franchise.

There is, however, one member of that crowd that absolutely deserved better: 1991's "The Rocketeer," in which Jennifer Connelly, Billy Campbell, and a rocket-powered jetpack faced off against Nazis in Los Angeles circa 1938.

One substantial difference that set "The Rocketeer" apart from the surrounding crop of pulp hero flicks was that its source material was actually pretty contemporary. Cliff Secord and his supporting cast were created in 1982 by the legendary comics creator Dave Stevens, and had been an indie favorite since its introduction. All things considered, Stevens produced a relatively small number of comics about the Rocketeer — his entire run with the character fits into a single 120-page hardcover — but his lavish, gorgeous art and incredible storytelling make it a timeless classic even today. Sadly, Stevens passed away in 2008 after a long battle with leukemia, which had long affected his output.

Recent findings suggest that there were real-life influences, too; in the film, the jetpack was created by Howard Hughes, and Timothy Dalton's villainous Neville Sinclair was based on actor (and real-life villain) Errol Flynn. Connelly's character, appropriately renamed Jenny, was based on Cliff's comics girlfriend Betty, who was in turn inspired by pin-up icon Bettie Page, of whom Stevens was a dedicated and unabashed fan.

As for the film, while it lacks the lushness of Stevens' comics art, it told the classic story of "boy loves girl, boy finds rocket pack, boy has to rescue girl from an evil Nazi actor played by one of the lesser James Bonds" in a fun, engaging way that made it a cult classic. It also has a connection to the modern Marvel Cinematic Universe. Two decades after "The Rocketeer," its director, Joe Johnston, would direct another, more successful retro-inspired superhero movie, 2011's "Captain America: The First Avenger.".

According to an interview with Stevens, the original blueprint for "The Rocketeer" had been to make a trilogy that would've skewed slightly more adult:.

According to recent reports, "So, we had a lot of interesting meetings with executives who passed on it but gave us some good criticisms. The last studio on the list was Disney. They took one look at it, and said 'toys!' So ... that's where we eventually made the deal. We originally signed on as a trilogy at Touchstone, the division of Disney doing more adult-themed films. [...] As soon as we all signed on, [Disney executive Jeffrey] Katzenberg pulled a switch and said, 'Nope, it's going to be a Disney release, because Disney needs a live-action hit.' So immediately, Betty and anything else "adult" went right out with the bathwater.".

We'll never know if a more adult-oriented version of "The Rocketeer" that kept elements like Betty's glamour modeling day job intact would've been successful enough to get us that trilogy, but the movie we got is well worth revisiting, even though it was crushed by "Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves" and "Terminator 2" at the box office.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shoes on or off?” Timothée Chalamet asks, like any good Newly introduced Yorker entering someone’s apartment. On is just fine.

Sources indicate that he’s carrying a white paper deli bag—“starving,” he claims—so I set him up at the dining table, where he unfurls a Lenwich Italiano. He devours it in less than two minutes. We’ve met before, but definitely never hung out at home. I think he’s friends with Frank Ocean, so I throw on Channel Orange. I had stocked up on a variety of beer and tea, can offer a coffee or a cocktail, but Chalamet wants Upcoming York City tap water, please, no ice.

Custom jacket by Haider Ackermann for Canada Goose; pants by Roa Hiking; backpack by Montbell.

Sources indicate that I live in a one-bedroom in the East 60s, the second floor of an 1870 town house. The walls are white, the floors are black, and there are flowers from the bodega on the coffee table.

Chalamet is in earth-toned gorpcore, from the sand-colored Gnuhr puffer all the way down to a tawny pair of Roas, and would look equally at home camouflaged on the streets of Manhattan or trekking in the Dolomites, which he has recently done with his father. Both ears are pierced. Except for a navy blue novelty tourist cap which reads, in a comically fancy font, “Hvar, Croatia”—another recent vacation destination, with girlfriend Kylie Jenner—Chalamet’s color palette is pure Arrakis.

THE PROPHECY Timothée Chalamet, who will reprise his role as Paul Atreides – the chosen one – in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, photographed in Iceland. Shirt by Prada.

According to recent reports, he’s just come from the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts, his alma mater located directly across the park, where he spoke with a group of drama students. Tonight he’s going to a Yankees game with his mom, the former New York City Ballet prima ballerina, and his sister, Pauline.

Late lunch concluded, he relocates to the sofa. “Ahhh,” he indicates, taking a big seat and resting his right arm along the back.

In a recent development, he glances down at the old issues of Vanity Fair on my coffee table and comes to a stop on one in particular: June 1995. Courtney Love is on the cover, photographed by Herb Ritts, wearing massive white-feathered wings in homage to the Nike of Samothrace at the Louvre. Inside, there’s a Ritts portrait of a toddler Frances Bean.

OUTDOOR VOICE Timothée Chalamet and photographer Aidan Zamiri spent three days in Iceland for this shoot, code-named Caladan—the planet where Chalamet’s Dune character, Paul Atreides, was born.

“This wasn’t the crazy one,” I say, guessing at what he’s thinking.

Three years prior to this cover, in the September 1992 issue of Vanity Fair, Lynn Hirschberg profiled Love and quoted her saying that she used heroin before and at the beginning of her pregnancy. The story sparked a crisis for the young Cobain family that resulted in an investigation by the department of children and family services and Cobain threatening Hirschberg and her dog. In the annals of celebrity profiles, it goes down as one of the most scalding of all time.

Chalamet knows all about that story because he’s seen Montage of Heck, the Cobain documentary that features the Vanity Fair article. “It was mind-blowing to me because Lynn has only ever been to me just a figure of warmth...” Chalamet claims, trailing off.

He puts the magazine back slowly, like it might burn him.

I’ll be honest with you: That’s not what’s about to happen here today. I’m not that scary, and he’s not using heroin. Nevertheless, this guy’s jumpy.

Recent findings suggest that it’s dangerous business for a movie star to open his mouth these days. Chalamet knows that better than anyone. At 30, he’s been famous his entire adult life. He’s dating one of the most visible women in the world. And he is acutely aware how a single comment in Vanity Fair could ricochet around the pinball machine of the internet. Earlier this year, during a no-holds-barred Oscar campaign for Marty Supreme, an offhand remark comparing the film industry to ballet and opera was met with outsize outrage, as some saw an opportunity to take Hollywood’s boy wonder down a peg. Those aware that he’s from a performing arts family knew what he meant. (“Is he wrong?” New York Times’ dance critic, Gia Kourlas, asked.) He doesn’t want to revisit that with me, perhaps because as he enters another awards season, he’s cautious in a way that only comes with experience.

In our 90 minutes together, Chalamet is both earnest and also reluctant to be profiled. He is by turns generous and guarded, confident and careful. He prefaces answers to no fewer than seven different questions by saying that he doesn’t want to sound “pretentious.” Truthfully, he never does. He’s protective of his personal life and will not discuss his girlfriend, nor much outside of filmmaking. “I wish I didn’t have to talk too much,” Chalamet claims. And yet here he is, all across Iceland in our cover shoot, and now on my blue velvet sofa.

Like every conversation in late 2026, ours starts with AI. “Thou shall not make a machine in the likeness of a man’s mind,” Chalamet reminds me, is one of the opening lines of Dune, Frank Herbert’s seminal 1965 sci-fi novel. The story takes place in a world where computers are banned long after an AI apocalypse like the ones that are presaged by current-day tech CEOs and causing so much societal agita.

COLD MOUNTAIN Chalamet formed a community while making the first two Dune films. The third was “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” Boots by Timberland; scarf by Norlha; vintage pants by Arc’teryx Pro.

In a recent development, chalamet tells me he’s reading The AGI Chronicles, tech journalist Kevin Roose’s latest book that maps out the sprint to reach artificial general intelligence. He points out that the first four chapters of the book track the plot of Artificial, referring to Luca Guadagnino’s new Sam Altman biopic. “This is five seconds ago.” He recommended the book to Marty Supreme director Josh Safdie, who later tells me Chalamet “found it to be not only informative, it’s helped with anxiety. The more you know, the less anxious you are about it.”.

Just when everyone seems at least a little bit anxious about the end of the human species, along comes Dune’s computer-free vision of the future that is, as Chalamet puts it, “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.”.

Recent findings suggest that LIFE ON MARS “The whole thing is daunting,” notes Chalamet about working on a franchise like Dune. Coat and shoes by Prada; pants by Stone Island.

According to recent reports, you don’t need to have seen the conclusion of Denis Villeneuve’s trilogy to understand a few things about it. First of all, that it is enormous. Its scale is even bigger than The Odyssey’s. The grand vision of Villeneuve’s intergalactic war drama actually makes the adaptation of the West’s first epic poem (and presumed best picture front-runner so far) look like an exercise in restraint.

The production design of Dune: Part Three, set 20,000 years in the future, is largely inspired by the pangeographical past. There are aesthetic references as far-ranging as the samurai and SEAL Team 6, the Roman Empire by way of the Third Reich, Islamic extremism and the Russian Orthodox Church, the Bedouins and the Asaro mud men of Papua Latest Guinea, and perhaps more than any other single culture, ancient Egypt. And like the pyramids themselves, the visual effect of the film is mystical rather than technological, even though both obviously are technical achievements. (No AI was used in the making of Dune: Part Three.).

Chalamet gives Villeneuve all the credit for what he calls the “titanic” scope of the film, constructed on the foundation of the first two over the course of a decade. “It seems like he just kept building and becoming more ferociously in control of it,” he notes. “Much like how Paul gets good at riding the sandworm, Denis took hold of these films.” The movie makes it easy to see how Star Wars—and particularly Anakin Skywalker’s character arc—is often considered derivative of Dune. (For the real heads: The story of Dune: Part Three is roughly equivalent to Star Wars episodes IV through VI, all in one film.).

According to recent reports, “It’s huge, huge geography,” Chalamet claims. “Do you think you could have done this when you were in your 30s?” Chalamet asked Villeneuve on set. “He goes, ‘No way.’ ” The director went on to tell him that he passed on a “huge sci-fi project” earlier in life that he wouldn’t even reveal to Chalamet, but Villeneuve “turned it down precisely because he felt like he didn’t have the tools yet.”.

It has been revealed that production designer Patrice Vermette’s life-size sets were so imposing that Chalamet spent time on location in Budapest ahead of the film’s shoot, immersing himself in the palace of Arrakis so that he wouldn’t be distracted by its grandeur when the cameras rolled. “The whole thing is daunting,” Chalamet says. “I didn’t want any part of the day to be lost to ‘Wow, look at what I’m stepping into,’ ” he adds later. Compared to shooting the first two Dune films, he was more or less alone on set. Chalamet remembers it as “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” The way Villeneuve puts it: “Timothée created a bubble around himself which allowed him to delve more deeply into the depressive darkness of his character.” He was, after all, preparing to play a murderer.

FIELD OF VISION According to Chalamet, Dune, which is set 20,000 years in a computer-free future, feels “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.” Hoodie and eye cover by Adon; T-shirt by James Perse Los Angeles; necklace by Blackmerle.

It has been revealed that part Three encounters Chalamet’s antihero, Duke Paul Atreides (also known by his Fremen alias Usul, as the religious cult figure Muad’Dib, and the Padishah Emperor of the known universe—you got all that?), at the height of his totalitarianism and the nadir of his soul. Sixty-one billion is the number of deaths attributable to Atreides, who in the Herbert novels compares himself to Adolf Hitler and Genghis Khan. He is a “psychopath,” according to Florence Pugh’s Princess Irulan. Villeneuve tells me there was another detached paranoid figure he compared Atreides to: Howard Hughes.

To get into character, Chalamet studied the personalities of world leaders—“everyone good and bad” and particularly “megalomaniacs across human history.” He notes that “Frank Herbert wrote Messiah to course correct...the first Dune, where Paul is sort of revered as a hero.” He continues: “This is a cautionary tale against cults of personality and figures of charisma.” When I ask if Donald Trump was on his mind, he indicates “not particularly,” noting that power and its corrosive effects on the soul are “eternally prescient themes.” The film is ultimately a story of atonement—if not redemption—for a fallen messiah.

Recent findings suggest that it was all this research that compelled Chalamet to shave off his globally recognized curly mop. “Decision fatigue is a real thing amongst the world leaders, good and bad, current and past.... The idea of not having to change clothes, not having to sweep the hair out of your face, simple shit like that.” And so Chalamet remarked goodbye to his Samson-like locks. Did he feel...“like Anne Hathaway in Les Mis?” Exactly. Or Natalie Portman in V for Vendetta, I offer. (He loves V for Vendetta.) Perhaps Demi Moore in G.I. Jane. “We would [shave] it basically every other day. My hair grows quickly, so we would get after it.” Today the curls, as you can see, have returned to their natural state. Power restored.

Recent findings suggest that “Timothée has become much more ambitious as an actor,” Villeneuve tells me when I ask how he’s changed in the decade that they’ve worked together. “He is exploring fresh artistic paths in a highly exciting way.” Costar Javier Bardem indicates, “In a way, his growth has been almost chronological with that of his character. In Dune: Part Three, there is a real gravitas to him. He stands firmly in his place, with a confidence and authority that he has earned through his work, his sacrifices, his dedication, and his commitment as an actor and as a professional. You can see it and feel it, and it is incredibly reaffirming to witness.”.

Safdie puts it like this: “I believe he’s like hi-fi sound. A good hi-fi system you can listen to in a tiny room and it makes the room feel huge. And he has that ability as an actor...his style of acting is larger-than-life realism.”.

“He is always restlessly searching to keep the scene alive,” says Greta Gerwig, who directed Chalamet in Lady Bird and Little Women.“He needs room to scream a scene or whisper it or jump up onto a table or pirouette.”.

According to recent reports, MAN OF ACTION Chalamet wants his art to speak for itself: “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there.” Suit by Gucci; shirt by Harvey Bigg.

According to recent reports, when I ask Chalamet if being famous his entire adult life prepared him to play a lonely-at-the-top emperor, he points to the moment in the first Dune when Paul and his mother, Lady Jessica, arrive on Arrakis and are greeted by the entire awe-inspiring army. “There were moments” in his own life, he says, when he realized about his relationship with the public: “Oh, something has shifted.”.

Sources indicate that wandering around my apartment, Chalamet is observant and interested. “The picture in your bathroom looks like Greta.” He means Gerwig, though it’s actually Edie Sedgwick balancing on one leg in arabesque, cigarette in hand. (Sedgwick lived in this apartment during her Warhol years, and the picture was taken in the living room where we are sitting.) We look through the 1965 problem of Vogue, in which the picture originally ran.

Industry observers note that he points out the French poster for The Graduate in the bedroom, in which a pink Matisse-like cutout of a woman’s elegant leg hovers in a thought bubble above Dustin Hoffman’s head. “I didn’t know it was called that,” he notes. “Le Lauréat.” (One journalist recommended that I speak French with Chalamet, as they find him more open when they do. Sadly, I can hardly order dinner in French.).

He loves an Annie Leibovitz picture of Cindy Sherman made up as the sad clown in Edward Hopper’s 1914 Soir Bleu and points out monographs about Ed Ruscha and Harmony Korine on my bookshelf. (“Beast!” he declares about Korine.).

He sweetly asks me about a picture of me officiating my best friends’ wedding.

WORLD VIEWS “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central,” claims Chalamet, a born and raised Upcoming Yorker.

We’re back on the sofa now. I’d asked Chalamet to do a little homework before our meeting: to come prepared to talk about his favorite movie performances. He was a diligent student, but instead came with four films and one play that specifically helped him get ready for his Vanity Fair cover shoot.

“Tree of Life,” he begins, citing Terrence Malick’s impressionistic masterpiece as the “biggest inspiration” for the cover shoot, photographed by Aidan Zamiri over three days in Iceland. “It could have been accomplished over a half day in the studio,” Chalamet notes, but they traveled thousands of miles because, as in Tree of Life, “the process is almost as vital as the finished product.”.

In a recent development, next up is One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. “It’s a kick-ass performance, and it’s provocative and heartwarming and full of life and one of the great movie performances of all time.” He cites Cloud Atlas, which the Wachowski sisters made years after The Matrix trilogy, as achieving the kind of scale that inspired the team to trek to the edge of Icelandic cliffs and inside waterfalls. (It’s also one of two films, along with Bruce Robinson’s 1987 Withnail and I, that Christopher Nolan has ever recommended to him.).

Chalamet whips out his orange iPhone—where he has incidentally started a new daily habit of playing chess—to show me the trailer for the Francis Ford Coppola–produced 1982 art house film Koyaanisqatsi, a hypnotic succession of increasingly uneasy urban vignettes, sped up and slowed down. “It’s about the humility you must feel as any person within the scale of the universe,” Chalamet indicates. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.” This one was recommended by Safdie and is clearly an inspiration for the relentless, kinetic pacing of his own movies as well. Chalamet is so close to Safdie that even the chess habit is inspired by the match that Safdie and Alfonso Cuarón continue in perpetuity.

“What’s interesting about Timmy is he’s incredibly curious and very sincere, but also has a pretty sharp sense of humor and can be quite jagged,” Safdie himself tells me a week later. “There’s a goofy seriousness to him. He likes to be provoked.”.

Industry observers note that SMOKE SHOW Next up for Chalamet? A top-secret collaboration with a “phenomenal” filmmaker. “It’s kind of a no-brainer.”.

Sources indicate that and finally, he gives me Man to Man, Tilda Swinton’s one-woman show presently on at London’s Royal Court Theatre. “It’s about the incredible futility of existence and a person losing their mind,” Chalamet states. “I liked it in this little program I created.”.

It has been revealed that I’ve never met any actor who prepared for a photo shoot the way he would for a role in a movie. I get the sense that’s just Chalamet’s way: Everything he does in public is considered part of the art. Everything except, perhaps, courtside appearances.

In a recent development, little provokes Chalamet more than the Newly introduced York Knicks, and it is the subject about which he gets most animated. “It’s the most quintessential New York team” for many reasons, he notes, but chief among them is location, location, location. “It’s not like the Yankees or Mets, Giants, or Jets. It’s in the heart of Manhattan, and it reflected the agony of the New York experience for decades.” Chalamet says he lives two lives: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.”.

When I ask what his greatest extravagance is, the immediate and definite answer is “sports tickets.” “Those away games weren’t cheap, but...it is the most fun I’ve had in my life as a human.” We know this. Because the best word to describe pictures of Chalamet courtside and in the Knicks locker room is simply ecstatic.

According to recent reports, he tells me about traveling through the night from San Antonio back to New York after the Game 5 championship as an all-time life high. “I flew with people that had been working at the Garden for decades,” he notes, explaining that Ben Stiller and Fat Joe were along for the ride on an MSG-owned plane. (“I don’t want to sound too out of touch,” he worries. I assure him the reader will understand that commercial airlines aren’t running 2 a.m. departures.) “It was just incredibly raucous, everyone celebrating.”.

DISTRESSED OUT Or is he? Chalamet isn’t pressed about trying to emulate his heroes: “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic.”.

According to recent reports, chalamet says he will always remember Jalen Brunson’s quiet leadership as the hallmark of the season overall. “It was not the cult of personality” you might expect to lead a championship team, he notes. “It was someone actually quite soft-spoken, reserved, and hardworking, and unassuming.”.

Recent findings suggest that on topics other than basketball, he is less enthusiastic. “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there,” he indicates. What’s something that no one asks you that you wish they would? “Nothing. I mean, nothing. I’m not being passive-aggressive about this interview at all, but I think...” he trails off. Chalamet points at the speaker, which is still playing Frank Ocean. “He’s one of the rare people where the vacuum of what’s out there about him helps drive the...” “Curiosity?” I offer. “Beyond curiosity, how brilliant his artistry is. But the economy of movies,” Chalamet says, thinking. “You got to sell a lot of tickets.”.

Which is exactly the reason that we’re sitting here together now. Who is his dream collaborator, living or dead? After a long silence, I tell him he can pass. “Okay. Pass.” What does he think of David Ellison’s Skydance taking over Warner Bros., the studio behind Dune? “I’m going to hit a Frank Ocean and be mysterious,” is all he indicates.

Industry observers note that leonardo DiCaprio once gave him very solid advice. Two rules: no superhero movies, no hard drugs. Would Chalamet have any advice for a 22-year-old getting started? “I think the best thing you can do is encourage people to be confident in what they believe is best for them.” Plus, he adds, “the Kane Parsons of it all brought me tremendous humility,” referencing the 21-year-old YouTuber turned director of the staggeringly successful Backrooms.

He’s vague about future projects. “I got one thing with a phenomenal filmmaker,” he says. “It’s kind of a no-brainer project, and should it get unveiled, I think you’ll see what I mean.”.

Sources indicate that would he ever return to the character of Elio, the protagonist of Call Me by Your Name that gave him his star turn? “A great question. Never say never, but...I’ve grown up with the mindset that you don’t really go near something that is so near and dear to people.” So, that’s a no. “Now, to work with Luca again? In a heartbeat.”.

GAME BOY As Chalamet sees it, there are two ways of living his life: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.” Jacket by Chrome Hearts; headlamp by Nitecore.

Is there any actor, or artist of any kind, after whose career he would like to model his own? “Who was [Bob] Dylan looking at? Dylan.” He broke the mold, I offer. “He created the mold.” Chalamet wants to be an original too (and perhaps this is what he meant when he declared that he was in “pursuit of greatness” at the 2025 SAG Awards). “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic,” he says. “Especially in the movie industry where people could feel like, Oh, that was the golden age.... You gotta cook it up in a unique way.”.

Around 6 p.m., Chalamet gets up off the couch and suits back up in his gorpcore. The Yankees game starts in just a couple of hours, and he has to shower and collect his mom and sister and make his way to the Bronx. I walk him downstairs, amble down the stoop, and almost want to say: Look! We survived!

Now that wasn’t so bad, was it?

#16479. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (638 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved.
  • In a recent development, once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything.
  • Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

In a recent development, once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:.

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

Industry observers note that it’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

It has been revealed that here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

In a recent development, and then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

Recent findings suggest that "Obsession" passed a box office milestone only five other horror films ever have when it crossed the $500 million mark. That would be an achievement regardless of its budget, but this movie only cost $600,000 to $750,000 to make. That means that when "Obsession" brought in $524.4 million by the end of its unprecedented box office run, it had made more than 500 times its budget.

In a recent development, for a while, that made "Obsession" the most profitable movie ever at the box office, until it was technically dethroned by the low-budget Chinese movie "Niu Lai." Still, it remains one of the most stunning horror success stories of recent years, which is especially impressive considering we've seen multiple low-budget horror movies become hits of late. But if you somehow managed to miss out on all of this, or just want to revisit one of the best horror movies of 2026, Netflix has you covered.

"Obsession" has a relatively simple premise, yet its execution and the lead performances elevate it beyond your typical low-budget horror fare. The film stars Michael Johnston as Baron "Bear" Bailey, a luckless music store worker who has a major crush on his friend/co-worker Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette). After buying a One Wish Willow toy, he wishes that Nikki loved him more than anyone in the world and gets everything he asked for and more. The only problem is, Nikki becomes absolutely obsessed with him, to the extent she's willing to hurt anyone who gets in her way.

Recent findings suggest that it's well worth doing so. "Obsession" is a confident crowd-pleaser with a killer lead performance from Navarette. In fact the actor's portrayal of Nikki proved to be her breakout turn, landing Navarrette a role as Rogue in the Marvel Cinematic Universe's upcoming "X-Men" movie reboot. No doubt, more high-profile roles await. As such, even if you're not too intrigued by the prospect of a twisted girlfriend causing violent chaos, you should at least check out "Obsession" to see one of the best performances of 2026 and the beginning of a star's ascendence. The film is streaming on Netflix as of November 17, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that I'm about to get into spoiler's for last week's "Million Dollar Moves" episode on the 2026 TV schedule, including who was eliminated, so heads up!
  • Hear me out, because I’m about to semi-talk some smack about the games Ali & Joanna and Anne-Marie & Riley have played, and I want to make it clear I like both teams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been very clear from the opening (express pass-oriented) episode of The Amazing Race 39 that producers were hoping for an all-women team to win. The season started out with five all-women teams, and subsequent episodes have noted various milestones the ladies have hit and more. On one level, it’s been nice to see so many ladies in the mix. Yet, because of the way gameplay has been set up, the same mixed gender teams were targeted myriad times, and that has meant two INCREDIBLE teams have not really being treated as threats.

Sources indicate that I'm about to get into spoiler's for last week's "Million Dollar Moves" episode on the 2026 TV schedule, including who was eliminated, so heads up! Still with me? Great.

Hear me out, because I’m about to semi-talk some smack about the games Ali & Joanna and Anne-Marie & Riley have played, and I want to make it clear I like both teams. They’re good TV. They’re strong competitors. I especially appreciate the likable personalities both teams have exhibited. The soccer pals and mother-daughter duo have great respect for their partners, but because of the way the latest season was put together and edited they have just skated by.

Because Ali & Joanna aligned with Ann-Marie & Riley early on, they’ve had a big advantage compared to a lot of other teams. I don’t think anyone is really on the look out for them, either, despite the fact both teams have earned a first place finish twice. They are threats, but because the mixed gender team of Michelle & Matt was highlighted as “the big threat” and went on a midseason three-episode winning tear, these other two teams have stayed under the radar.

Listen, I feel like The Amazing Race producers knew Matt & Michelle would be targeted in the double U-Turn, but they and Daisha and Dalton prevailed anyway during that first live round. Then, the next week they set up a second double U-Turn, and of course Matt & Michelle were targeted again. Phil called the couple “dynamic” in this BTS Race video, and given how fun they were to watch, I wish things would have shaken out a bit differently so another (or other) teams were targeted that second episode, but that is what it is.

In a recent development, the bigger problem, however? The way the challenge was set up led to all of the other teams working together. Everyone huddled together and gave each other answers like they were cheating on a pop quiz, and then Matt & Michelle had to go it alone. They also had to do both sides of the challenge with no help. Yes, struggling with directions didn’t help, but they were at a heavy disadvantage due to being targeted. The other teams weren’t.

I’m sure TAR would call it fair gameplay. I call it boring TV.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

The thing is, as a former soccer player myself, I get the competitive attitude, and I’d love to see Ali & Joanna win. I’ve actually felt that way even before Michelle & Matt started dominating. I think it’s probably a strength for the two leading lady teams they’re both just skating by under-the-radar this season. If I were them, I’d be extremely happy about this outcome and the way the show has ultimately set them up for success.

I honestly more blame the set up of the race this season for creating a non-compelling narrative. Allowing teams to “work together” has been a point of contention on The Amazing Race for a long time. (Like I can remember a major incident back in Season 32, so years, and producers have even discussed making changes before.).

Recent findings suggest that there’s always a question of “where is the line,” right? Is it OK to give another team directions or point them in the right direction with a clue? I’d argue yes. Is it OK to work together on a detail-oriented counting challenge 100% so that the colluding teams all finish together? Even if the Race says that’s fine, I’d argue those episodes make the show go from a 9/10 to a 2/10 for those who are watching.

Just something to consider, Race producers.

According to recent reports, anyway, this “working together” philosophy has certainly helped Ali & Joanna and Ann-Marie & Riley get through a lot of challenges this season, and they’ve managed to do it with most of the other teams being none the wiser, or at least not seeing them as real threats to win. There's a lot of money at stake, and per TAR’s rules, they aren’t doing anything wrong. Still, if an all-women team wins this season, I would have liked it way better if they’d done it on their own merit, and not because of some Amazing Race challenge loopholes.

#16473. 5 Reasons Why Robert Pattinson Could Be The Best James Bond Yet

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1558 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashfilm ↗ Open Full Page

5 Reasons Why Robert Pattinson Could Be The Best James Bond Yet

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond, beating out several promising contenders to take the coveted role.
  • Thus far, Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with both excitement and wariness — which is to be expected.
  • In a recent development, the "Primetime" star has been delivering consistently compelling performances for years now, and if nothing else it will be fascinating to see what he does to make England's greatest spy his own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond, beating out several promising contenders to take the coveted role. Denis Villeneuve will oversee the upcoming 26th Bond installment, and he couldn't have chosen a more dynamic and interesting leading man.

Thus far, Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with both excitement and wariness — which is to be expected. After all, the British actor is one of the biggest stars in Hollywood and is therefore unlike any actor to be cast in the role throughout the franchise's more than 60-year history. But clearly Villeneuve and upcoming Bond custodians Amazon MGM have been impressed by the actor, and frankly it's not hard to see why.

In a recent development, the "Primetime" star has been delivering consistently compelling performances for years now, and if nothing else it will be fascinating to see what he does to make England's greatest spy his own. Sure, on the surface he seems like a safe choice — A-lister white guy with a string of hits to his name. But part of what makes Pattinson so exciting as an actor is his unpredictability. Beyond that, there are myriad reasons why he could not only make a great 007, but might just give us the best Bond yet. Here are five of them.

Robert Pattinson is a major star with the kind of look you'd associate with James Bond. But he's made no secret of the fact he's also a bit of a weirdo underneath it all, and in that sense he shares something in common with Bond.

Industry observers note that 007 is a similarly deceptive character. Like Pattinson, he's a refined, handsome white guy with an urbane manner. But in the first Bond book, "Casino Royale," author Ian Fleming described him as a "blunt instrument." That element has been integral to the character since his inception. That is to say, Bond is much more than a posh boy with a licence to kill. He's damaged, troubled, maybe a little rough around the edges. Sure, his cinematic history has proved the character lends himself to interpretation, but the best Bond performances have integrated that dark side to some extent.

Pattinson could give us the best version of that to date. Remember that short film he made for GQ about his mounting anxiety over leaving his hotel room to get a hotdog? Something's up with this guy in the best way possible, and every role he's taken since then has been testament to that fact. From his lecherous, questionably-accented preacher in "The Devil all the Time" to his delightfully unhinged nineteenth-Century lighthouse keeper in "The Lighthouse," Pattinson has clearly been having a ball playing crazy (and that's not to mention some of his most Pattinsoniest performances in films such as "Good Time" and "The King"). He'll have to keep it under control for Bond, but 007 needs an edge to be interesting, and Pattinson has a wild unpredictability could be the best thing to ever happen to the character.

Sources indicate that robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of unknown actors being given the role. For Bond purists, such a thing is basically sacrilegious. For everyone else, it might just be the most exciting thing to happen to Bond since 1962's "Dr. No" kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise.

Industry observers note that look, there's a chance Pattinson could be distracting as 007. Bond is a male fantasy come to life, and part of the series' success could well be attributed to the fact it's easier for audiences to project themselves onto relative unknowns. On the other hand, it only takes one Bond movie for an actor to become a major star, so there'll always be diminishing returns in that respect. What's more, I think it's fair to say we need major changes after the multiple duds that characterized Daniel Craig's last few years as Bond. The franchise was in danger of becoming less relevant than it once was, and casting a star of Pattinson's standing, in a movie directed by the similarly esteemed Denis Villeneuve is a way to remind people of the saga's blue chip status.

It has been revealed that what's more, we're not talking about any A-lister here. Pattinson has proved time and again he has the ability to completely disappear into a role. So, what we're actually getting is an actor with the gravitas and appeal of a megastar who is simultaneously able to become a cinematic cipher onto which we can all project our fantasies of becoming the most lethal instrument the Secret Intelligence Service has at its disposal. As the first millennial Bond, and the first major star to take on the role, Pattinson could prove to be a master stroke of casting on Villeneuve's part.

There was a major turning point in Robert Pattinson's career whereby he seemed to throw caution to the wind and embrace the most challenging, unusual, and downright insane roles he could. In 2017, the year "Good Time" debuted, GQ exclaimed that "the upcoming Rob Pattinson is defined by his willingness to go berserk or go home." Ever since then he has delivered back to back unforgettable performances that have seen the middle class London boy disappear into some of the most unique characters to appear on-screen in the last decade.

According to recent reports, part of it was an attempt to escape the shadow of the "Twilight" saga, with which he'd made his name. But his portrayals of these more off-kilter characters that came in the wake of his decision to recalibrate felt so natural and honest that it was like he was finally able to be himself, paradoxically by playing people so completely unlike himself.

What's even more impressive is that he hasn't slowed down since deciding to "go berserk." 2026 saw him deliver yet another electric performance in the dark, unsettling media satire thriller "Primetime," in which he completely disappeared behind the mask of "To Catch a Predator" host Chris Hanson. Pattinson just can't seem to deliver a bad performance. Wild, sure. Unpredictable? Absolutely. But he's never been anything less than magnetic and seems incapable of being boring. That should be hugely exciting for James Bond fans.

"Tenet" was full of confusing moments but Robert Pattinson's ability to portray a debonair spy with a quietly simmering intensity was not in question. The actor played Neil in Christopher Nolan's thriller. A mysterious operative who helps John David Washington's Protagonist throughout the film, Neil possesses all the charisma of James Bond and even seems to have a bit of a dark side.

All you need to see to be convinced Pattinson has what it takes to play Bond is the scene in which Neil scopes out the freeport where he prepares to steal a priceless art piece. As he's shown around the facility, Pattinson's agent simultaneously exudes a polite charm and a kind of palpable ruthlessness, smiling at his tour guide before staring intently at possible escape routes and security measures. You can feel the cogs turning as he looks around, with Pattinson managing to convey a real sense of Neil's thought processes. When he's told about the freeport's security system, which sucks the air out of a room within 10 seconds, he simply claims "Blimey," an ironic understatement accompanied by a wry smile more than worthy of 007.

Surely nobody ever doubted Pattinson could play an urbane sleuth who looks remarkably sharp in a suit. But his "Tenet" performance hints at something more interesting. The brief moments when Pattinson's agent drops the charming facade and focuses his attention on various parts of the building's design convey a cold, calculating intensity that bodes well for a Bond with a truly dark side. Nolan's confounding thriller is an exciting proof of concept for Pattinson's Bond and his ability to exude both charisma and a striking cold-bloodedness unlike any 007 yet seen on-screen.

In a recent development, if you were told Robert Pattinson went to Eton and Oxford you probably wouldn't have a hard time believing it. He didn't, but it feels like he'd be very much at home in the public school boy milieu. That's interesting because while previous James Bond actors have managed to affect that kind of high-born aura, Pattinson is the first to just sort of have it from the get go.

In a recent development, he's an upper-middle class white Londoner with a Received Pronunciation accent and an urbane, sophisticated manner. Sure, he's also the guy who can't stop nervously laughing in interviews and who seems to run on pure anxiety most of the time. But there's no denying he has the sort of heritage you'd associate with Bond.

Roger Moore — the only other London-born actor to play Bond — had something similar, but undercut it with his famously tongue-in-cheek portrayal. Sean Connery was, of course, Scottish, Timothy Dalton was born in Wales, Pierce Brosnan is Irish, and Daniel Craig is from Chester in North England. Each of them brought something unique to the role, but of all the James Bond actors Pattinson seems like the first who won't have to work too hard at exuding the kind of aura we've come to expect from a character Idles frontman Joe Talbot described as a "murderous toff.".

Take a look.

It has been revealed that the perched bird really fits into the vibe the ladies of Panem have created in recent weeks. Mckenna Grace has dropped all the Hunger Games looks, and paid homage to Jennifer Lawrence many times. Elle Fanning has gotten into the Capitol-themed dressing in recent weeks. The whole thing has been really fun to watch play out. Now, Whitney Peak, who plays Haymitch’s “love” Lenore Dove – herself a mirror to Lucy Gray – has her own viral look.

Industry observers note that of course, even when you are wearing a gorgeous deep blue gown with perfect theming and an intricate shoulder, it’s hard to compete with the fan service of seeing the OGs on a Hunger Games carpet again. It’s difficult to believe it’s been 11 years since the last Katniss Everdeen story graced the major screen, but time has passed. The cast still looks great, though.

It has been revealed that suzanne Collins’ return to Panem with Sunrise on the Reaping was an exceptionally well-reviewed (if a bit bleak) book. The trailer for Reaping has looked astounding and first reactions are coming in. The movie officially hits the 2026 release schedule on November 20th, and while this was the significant premiere, I hope that means we have a couple more days of fun celebrity fashion to go.

#16471. The Hunger Games Officially Changes Genres With a Near-Perfect New Movie

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (896 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Polygon ↗ Open Full Page

The Hunger Games Officially Changes Genres With a Near-Perfect New Movie

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Hunger Games has never been afraid to put its young characters through the wringer.
  • More than a decade after the first film debuted, the franchise remains as relevant as ever, especially as our real world continues to look more and more like the dystopian nation of Panem.
  • Industry observers note that sunrise on the Reaping follows 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), a charming and hard-working boy from District 12, the poorest district in Panem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Hunger Games has never been afraid to put its young characters through the wringer. Despite being one of the most successful book and film franchises in history, the source material always stays true to its bleak premise: this is a story where teen bodies are used to keep the public under control.

More than a decade after the first film debuted, the franchise remains as relevant as ever, especially as our real world continues to look more and more like the dystopian nation of Panem. In 2023, we got a movie, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, exploring the backstory of the franchise’s main villain, President Snow. Francis Lawrence’s Sunrise on the Reaping, his fifth Hunger Games movie, is a direct sequel to that story, and while it’s still YA, he and his team push the boundaries of what we can expect from the genre. The result is an incredibly entertaining blockbuster with the feel of a bleak, existential horror movie.

Industry observers note that sunrise on the Reaping follows 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), a charming and hard-working boy from District 12, the poorest district in Panem. To make ends meet and take care of his mom and little brother, he illegally distills and sells moonshine. He spends his free time with his girlfriend, Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), even though her family doesn’t approve of him.

Sources indicate that the story picks up on Reaping Day. This year is special, marking the 50th annual Hunger Games. To celebrate, the Capitol is demanding four tributes per district instead of two. After a boy’s name is called out and he runs off in fear, the reaping devolves into chaos. The boy gets shot, and Haymitch gets involved, trying to protect Lenore Dove from some Peacekeepers. To keep the show going and capture footage the Capitol can air, Haymitch is selected as the substitute tribute, and his journey begins.

If this all feels familiar, it should. While the Capitol comes off as particularly calculating, with the film paying close attention to how Snow (Ralph Fiennes) and his associates doctor footage for their own ends, Lawrence still follows the formula established by the original films. It isn’t until kids start dying before the Games begin that you realize Sunrise on the Reaping is doing something else. This is not a survival story; we all know where Haymitch ends up. This is a story about watching a character lose everything they care about.

Industry observers note that while The Hunger Games movies always feature amazing actors, the cast for Sunrise on the Reaping is almost comically stacked. Fiennes brings his particular brand of menace to Coriolanus Snow, a character who develops a fixation on Haymitch. Glenn Close plays Drusilla Sickle, a Capitol escort sent to accompany the District 12 tributes (twist: she hates her job and the kids). Jesse Plemons takes over Plutarch Heavensbee from the late Philip Seymour Hoffman, playing him as aloof but quietly committed as he juggles making the show the Capitol wants and keeping Snow happy, all while fostering a rebellion among the tributes. At the center of it all is Zada, featured in almost every scene as he communicates an escalating sense of doom, loss, and despair.

Panem also gets a ’70s-style makeover. The Capitol is pushed decades into the past without losing its futuristic sheen, landing somewhere close to The Jetsons (complimentary). The best set is saved for what matters: the arena. It’s an open green field, lush and full of color, clear rivers, and adorable bunnies and deer. It’s a trick, though. The water is poisonous, and the animals are under the Capitol’s control. One tribute is killed by a swarm of squirrels. Another is impaled through the throat by a bird with a long, needle-thin beak. Haymitch’s blueprint to enter the arena and humiliate the Capitol on live TV is stymied at every turn, and Snow punishes him by making sure Haymitch gets a front seat to his friends’ deaths, one by one.

Sunrise on the Reaping is a tragedy. If you’ve seen the previous films, you know that Haymitch is an alcoholic from District 12, reviled by his community, and that it takes him meeting Katniss and forming a friendship with her for him to finally thaw. Sunrise on the Reaping effectively fills in the blanks of his character. At times, I found myself thinking, “There’s no way this could get worse,” but the film consistently proves me wrong.

In a recent development, it’s no secret that Sunrise on the Reaping also features the return of Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson. It’s a sweet moment for fans, but also the weakest part of the film, muddling an otherwise thoughtful and engaging blockbuster with bad wigs and nostalgia. The cameos feel like reassurance that there’s a light at the end of the tunnel for Haymitch, undercutting the dread that Lawrence was so committed to building in the first place.

Still, Sunrise on the Reaping is the most depressing Hunger Games movie yet; Katniss and Peeta had it easy. And while it has the franchise’s blockbuster magic, it adds a welcome dose of dread and tragic inevitability, easily elevating it to one of the series’ best movies.

Sources indicate that the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping premieres in theaters Nov. 20.
