📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A grimmer, gloomier “Hunger Games” is on the horizon with “Sunrise on the Reaping,” adapted from Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel about the origin story of the hardened alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy. Here, the teenage version of Woody Harrelson’s character in the original films is played by Australian actor Joseph Zada, the blond, ringletted Adonis who also starred as the moody Cal Trask in the recent “East of Eden” series.

Franchise fans might be riveted by Francis Lawrence’s latest installment — points for consistency, as he’s directed all the films dating back to 2013’s “Catching Fire” — but those audiences not already invested in the dystopian material and tales of tributes will find themselves left out in the cold by an overlong (it’s 158 minutes, so get comfortable), visually soupy, and narratively morose reprisal. But no matter, as this fresh slice of bankable I.P. is likely to rake in a hysterical amount of money, and perhaps launch Zada’s career as a face of new Hollywood stardom. Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier.

Industry observers note that the film is set during the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. Only 16 years old, Haymitch is thrust into games that are rigged from the start — and whose broadcasting is ultimately edited and deepfaked to look like pro-Capitol propaganda. (The film nudges a little bit toward the ethics of state surveillance and how footage can be manipulated or even fabricated for political ends.) His pastoral, if impoverished, life in District 12 is small but happy, with girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) and a mother and younger brother (Kara Tointon and Smylie Bradwell) with whom he shares close affinity, plus a best friend we’ll eventually find out will become the father of Katniss Everdeen (Lawrence) in the later films.

In a recent development, after a reaping (refresher: that’s when tributes are selected ceremonial-style, here as by a grotesquely pulled-tight-in-the-face Glenn Close as Drusilla Sickle) turns bloody, long-shot Haymitch ends up being selected at only 16. Violence follows him everywhere, as during the subsequent Tribute Parade, tragedy strikes Haymitch’s childhood friend (Molly McCann) during a horse-drawn Tribute chariot ride. Sequences meant to be thrilling often lack connective tissue to the rest of the material, or are devised in such a maelstrom of CGI (as goopy and cacophonous as a Marvel battle) that it’s difficult to feel engaged. It’s also unhelpful that most of the supporting cast is so wildly over the top, especially Capitol residents played by Close and a smarmy and mannered Kieran Culkin. Jesse Plemons as a Hunger Games camera operator brings a shade of moral dimension to the proceedings, but as with his “Digger” role, the actor feels woefully underused. Ralph Fiennes as Capitol president Snow, meanwhile, is given but scraps of material to work with.

In a recent development, the by-the-book script by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie appears to stick faithfully to Collins’ 2025 novel, with plenty of potential for visual appeal that goes largely unrealized. The Hunger Games arena Haymitch is thrust into is rife with hidden dangers: poisonous streams, a deadly force field, and other trippy flora and fauna that vibe like a dark mirror version of “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” but again, “Sunrise on the Reaping” trips up on the CGI fakery.

Industry observers note that the movie’s stacked young cast of tributes and mentors (those victors of previous Hunger Games tournaments) includes Mckenna Grace as a District 12 tribute who’s not to be trusted, the endearingly wily Ben Wang (recently excellent in the SXSW film “Brian”), plus a gravely underused Maya Hawke as the winner of the 49th Hunger Games, Kelvin Harrison Jr. as victor of the 34th, and the great Lili Taylor as a legacy tribute played previously by Lynn Cohen (aka Magda on “Sex and the City”) in the second film. These characters mostly exist to introduce themselves to Haymitch, be established as good or evil or helpful or unhelpful, and then be shuffled out of the scene. Elle Fanning is rather amusing, however, as the Capitol stylist Effie Trinket, styled and nearly drowned out by extremely outré fashions. Glenn Close also (with a visage channeling Katherine Helmond as Ida Lowry in “Brazil”) could’ve been used to better effect.

It has been revealed that the specter of death looming over the film should not be confused for much in the way of actual depth, and while Zada’s performance is charming enough, his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films. He feels like a cog or a function to get this prequel to line up with the prior films — and isn’t that what he is? Which makes the movie, and ergo probably the book, feel a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series’ lore. When Haymitch comes home from Second Quarter Quell and descends into depression and alcoholism, that’s when the movie gets most interesting. Not a great sign when your film’s tepid coda is also its best moment.

And equally worrying is a series of cameos tacked onto the film’s end that smack of depressing fan service. These movies seem to be mostly critic-proof and hugely appealing to their core audience, but “Sunrise on the Reaping” is a dreary slog, another death-march “They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?” riff with a pretty Gen Z cast, and one that mistakes new layers of darkness (and trauma!) for the sort of profundity that its filmmakers hope will burnish a creatively withering property.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens in theaters on Friday, November 20.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1032 w)

How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The dark web isn't just for illicit activities.
  • Industry observers note that but this also provides perfect cover for criminals and hackers who create clones of legitimate dark web sites to steal sensitive data and cryptocurrency from privacy-conscious owners.
  • Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The dark web isn't just for illicit activities. In fact, many legitimate online platforms maintain a ".onion" domain on the dark web for privacy reasons, including media outlets like ProPublica and BBC News, social media sites like Facebook, and privacy-conscious communication platforms like Proton Mail and SecureDrop.

Industry observers note that but this also provides perfect cover for criminals and hackers who create clones of legitimate dark web sites to steal sensitive data and cryptocurrency from privacy-conscious owners. And given that onion links are long and jumbled, it’s easy for users to accidentally click on the wrong link and end up on a fake website instead of the real one. When the FBI seized 276 onion addresses during 2014's Operation Onymous, they found that 153 of them were phishing sites.

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

Sources indicate that while phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

Sources indicate that when you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

Recent findings suggest that for example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives people a false sense of security.

Industry observers note that of course, most dark web consumers don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

It has been revealed that of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

Recent findings suggest that there are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

Sources indicate that the Tor Project has a feature called Onion-Location, which lets clear web websites advertise that they have a dark web version available for users who prefer more privacy. If opening a regular TLS-backed website using the Tor Browser reveals a purple “onion available” button in the address bar, you can click on it and be redirected to the official onion link associated with that site.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

Recent findings suggest that when you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Recent findings suggest that don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Industry observers note that also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

For people, this can make a difference when travelling abroad on expensive roaming data, topping up a prepaid blueprint or running low on a monthly data bundle. Data Saver can also help when browsing on a weak connection.

While the press release didn’t go into detail on the privacy aspects of the feature, it did note that “the feature is optional, and people can switch it on or off and see how much data they have saved.”.

#16391. Why Clemenza Didn't Return For The Godfather Part II

📅 26 May 2024 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1169 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Screenrant ↗ Open Full Page

Why Clemenza Didn't Return For The Godfather Part II

📅 26 May 2024 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Godfather Part II continued the story of Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) after becoming the fresh Don of the Corleone family, and while most of the cast from the first movie returned, the character Peter Clemenza was notably absent.
  • In a recent development, in 1972, Francis Ford Coppola brought what’s now considered one of the greatest movies of all time and the best in the gangster genre: The Godfather.
  • The Godfather introduced viewers to the Corleone family in New York City, led by Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Godfather Part II continued the story of Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) after becoming the fresh Don of the Corleone family, and while most of the cast from the first movie returned, the character Peter Clemenza was notably absent. Played by Richard S. Castellano, Clemenza was one of Vito’s caporegimes and oldest and most trusted friends, who was instrumental in Michael cementing his power, and his absence was conspicuous.

In a recent development, in 1972, Francis Ford Coppola brought what’s now considered one of the greatest movies of all time and the best in the gangster genre: The Godfather. Based on Mario Puzo’s 1969 novel of the same name, and with a screenplay co-written by Puzo and Coppola, The Godfather was a massive critical and commercial success and made way for one of the greatest movie trilogies of all time.

The Godfather introduced viewers to the Corleone family in New York City, led by Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando). When Vito decided to hand over his empire to his youngest son, Michael, conflict with the rest of the city’s crime families was triggered, putting the lives of Vito’s loved ones in great danger, while Michael was pushed to take the lead despite staying out of the family business his whole life. The Godfather was followed by two sequels, and though most of the cast returned in The Godfather Part II, Castellano’s Clemenza didn’t come back.

Throughout The Godfather, Clemenza was tasked with getting rid of some of the Corleone family’s enemies, most notably Don Victor Stracci during the infamous “baptism killings” and he planted the gun for Michael to use to kill Sollozzo and McCluskey.

In a recent development, the Godfather Part II arrived just two years after The Godfather, and is obviously both a sequel and a prequel, picking up the story of Michael now as the fresh Don of the family while also going back in time to explore the origin story of Vito. The “present” timeline notably didn’t include Clemenza, which was strange given his strong connection to the Corleone family and his place as one of their most trusted capos.

According to recent reports, coppola said in a DVD documentary (via Mental Floss) that Castellano had declined to return as he wanted more money and dialogue approval. The latter demand came after he ad-libbed the now-famous “take the cannoli” line in the first movie at the urging of his wife, Ardell Sheridan. However, Castellano denied this in an interview in 1981 (via New York Post) and explained he didn’t return in The Godfather Part II as he disagreed with how Clemenza had been written.

Recent findings suggest that according to Castellano, the original script had Clemenza testifying against the Corleone family, which he - quite rightly - claimed was completely off-character. Castellano added that the demands on him were “impossible” as he had settled on a price, and he was required to gain weight after losing 194 pounds to play young Clemenza. He also claimed Coppola promised to tell the press he had turned down the role for artistic reasons, but Coppola ended up saying something entirely different.

Sources indicate that despite Castellano not returning to play Clemenza in the present timeline in The Godfather Part II, Coppola found a way to give him closure and fill in that space. Bruno Kirby was cast as young Clemenza for the flashback scenes to Vito’s backstory, and in the present timeline, Clemenza was killed off-screen, with the betrayal of the Corleone family given to someone else. Fredo mentioned that Clemenza died of a heart attack, but Cicci implied he might have been murdered.

In a recent development, ultimately, Clemenza was replaced by Frank Pentangeli (Michael V. Gazzo), who was given the storyline of testifying against the Corleone family. It was a smart move: seeing Clemenza betray the Corleone family would have felt like too much of a swerve, even if it also felt strange not seeing him in The Godfather Part II. Pentangeli was, instead, retroactively established as another long-term Corleone capo who had worked with Vito in his early career in the olive oil business.

In a recent development, having been a key figure under Clemenza's leadership running the Corleone's family operations in New York, Pentangeli inherits the operation, kicking off an almost-immediate set of conflicts as he seeks to consolidate his position, but Michael refuses to allow him to take out his rivals, the Rosato brothers. Because of Michael's keenness to establish strong relations with Hyman Roth (Lee Strasberg), who is aligned with the Rosatos, he refuses, and Pentangeli is incensed by the insult.

Pentangeli promptly becomes the heart of the story as the walls close in on Michael and the Senate hearing investigating organized crime and allegations of his crimes threaten to crumble his empire. Gazzo's performance is great, and earned him a Best Supporting Actor nomination at the Oscars - which he ultimately lost to Robert De Niro for the same movie, understandably. Any other year, he would have had a strong chance of winning.

Even with the Rosato brothers and Roth pulling the strings, it would never have worked for Clemenza to be the one to betray the Corleones: it had to be someone like Pentangeli, who inherited his power, and like Michael, immediately faced a challenge. Those underworld politics were a great foundation for the entire subplot, which ultimately saw Michael using Frank's brother Vincenzo to intimidate him into recanting his Senate statement in fear. It's at this point that Gazzo really earns his plaudits, and his arc subtly reflecting Michael's own precarious position in the first movie only works because of how well he sells it all.

Sources indicate that ultimately, Robert Duvall's Tom Hagen using Frank's knowledge of Roman history and how traitors' families would be spared if they killed themselves is a brilliant, chilling end to his story, and reveals both the dark morality of this world and the complex parallel with Ancient Rome. There's also an incredibly compelling mystery left unanswered, which was only explained in the original script: Frank's children were under Vincenzo's protection in Sicily, and his brother turning up was supposed to be a reminder not to betray his blood oath and the Mafia's code of silence, or retribution would be taken on his kids.

Sources indicate that it's an unfortunate cut, but the fact that Gazzo's performance so thoroughly convinces of the threat without it ever having to be spelled out is the final testimony to how great he was as Clemenza's replacement. Ultimately, Castellano's unwillingness to sign on for the sequel may have led to the loss of a great character, but it worked out better for The Godfather Part II.

The Godfather Part II is a continuation of the Corleone crime family saga. The film explores Vito Corleone's early life in Sicily and 1910s Latest York, while Michael Corleone navigates the 1950s, seeking to expand the family's influence into Las Vegas, Hollywood, and Cuba.

  • These include a vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages, as well as another that could allow a malicious Bluetooth device to pair without user interaction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While the first HomeView units won’t reach customers until tomorrow, Apple today released a software update addressing nine security vulnerabilities. Here are the details.

Apple today released HomeView Software Version 27.2 (build 24V526), which contains some of the security fixes the company included in recent updates to its other operating systems, including iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, and iPadOS 27.2.

These include a vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages, as well as another that could allow a malicious Bluetooth device to pair without user interaction.

In practice, this means that consumers who get the device starting tomorrow are advised to update it as soon as possible, since the vulnerabilities have been publicly disclosed.

Here’s the full security content of HomeView Software Version 27.2.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts.

Description: A logic concern was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data.

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory.

Description: A use-after-free matter was addressed with improved memory management.

Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption.

Description: An out-of-bounds write problem was addressed with improved input validation.

Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction.

Description: This matter was addressed with improved checks.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction.

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher.

Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages.

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation.

#16388. Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1226 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Indiewire ↗ Open Full Page

Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A willingness to die for sex is a familiar bargain for queer people.
  • It has been revealed that but a more twisted and nervy dance between desire and death has unfolded in this year’s spate of particularly macabre queer films.
  • This alarm has played out, perhaps most obviously, in horror films.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A willingness to die for sex is a familiar bargain for queer people. Born in the twentieth century at the wrong place and time? Beware of Nazis, AIDS, and other mortal dangers. Hollywood has at times depicted these threats in ways that emphasize the humanity of LGBTQ+ people, as when Tom Hanks played a lawyer dying of AIDS in “Philadelphia,” during the height of the epidemic in 1993. The industry also has a history of finding ever more creative ways to kill off and scapegoat queer characters, a trope that as recently as 10 years ago seemed to be running amok.

It has been revealed that but a more twisted and nervy dance between desire and death has unfolded in this year’s spate of particularly macabre queer films. After years of what felt like permanent advances in rights and representation, LGBTQ+ people have been stung by backlash, including attacks on gender-affirming care, legal threats to marriage equality, and cuts to suicide prevention. Amid a reduced perception of safety, anxieties about the possibilities and consequences of nonnormative desire are spilling out onscreen like so much fake blood. Even so, their formulation is evidence of social and creative progress. Related Stories ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They? ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie.

This alarm has played out, perhaps most obviously, in horror films. In Adrian Chiarella’s “Leviticus” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” same-sex attraction engenders extreme and potentially deadly terror, be it from detractors or the people it consumes. Both films explore not the evils of queerness — an argument that belongs to the tradition of queer-coded villains — but the horrors of having one’s desires villainized.

The year’s queer history films also subvert conventional narratives around sexuality and deadly fates. In Andrew Scott’s awards-season vehicle “Elsinore,” Ian Charleson’s dying wish to play Hamlet is one many actors would share; the film doesn’t focus on how or why he has AIDS, but what he wants to do before it kills him. The Spanish epic “La Bola Negra” depicts forbidden romance, but desire isn’t what dooms its multiple generations of queer men. The fact that they’re swept up in the currents of history, just like everyone else, is part of the film’s revolutionary power.

The era for combatting the notion that being gay is a no good, very bad thing in a straightforward way finally seems to have passed. Usually such sermons were preaching to the choir anyway. Gone is the teary earnestness of a conversion therapy drama like “Boy Erased,” from 2018, in which much of the trauma wrought on Lucas Hedges’ character derives from the church but is carried out by earthly messengers. In “Leviticus,” when a healer tries to pray the gay away from a pair of lovesick adolescents, he conjures supernatural and murderous doppelgangers.

After rituals of deliverance are performed over the convulsing bodies of a pair of schoolmates (played by Joe Bird and Stacy Clausen), each one is haunted by an illusion of the other that tries to kill them. The concept of “Leviticus,” named for the Old Testament book that forbids man to lie with man, partly functions as a wry play on the idea that you never get over your first crush. It also takes the fear that so many queer people know well — that what you desire most will be your downfall — to literal and horrifying extremes. Imagining the bigotry of organized religion as a senselessly violent supernatural force is a radical reversal. The boys aren’t the problem; the boogeymen that torment them spring from the so-called good book.

Industry observers note that schoenbrun’s meta queer fantasia “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” likewise performs a canonical revision. The nonbinary killer in the campy franchise within the film were themselves killed and sunk to the bottom of a lake by their comically gender-panicked peers. A victim seeking revenge, the TV-headed slasher is called Little Death, a nod to a French term for orgasm, la petite mort. Hannah Einbinder’s millennial filmmaker is on a quest to reboot the franchise, but more significantly, to achieve her own “little death.” In order to grow more comfortable with sex, and give into her own desires, her fear of intimacy — one that, again, many queer people know well — needs to be killed.

The movie ultimately intertwines fear of death with the fear of intimacy in a way that demonstrates the stakes — how you can feel so afraid of getting close to someone you could just die. But what must be slaughtered in this case is fear itself — so that same-sex desire, which has so often been pathologized and villainized, can flourish. (The trail of straight people extravagantly dispatched along the way, like so many gays before them, is one of the film’s many deranged and delightful flourishes.).

There is a potent realignment evident in the year’s period films as well, which center the desires and fates of queer characters on their own terms, rather than taking their oppression or disease as subjects unto themselves. “Elsinore” leans a bit heavily on obvious sentiment while leaving much of the thematic richness of “Hamlet” on the table. But Charleson’s determination to play the part before he dies is what drives the film, while the indignities of succumbing to AIDS are mostly a secondary plot.

Contrast that with recent period dramas on TV, like “It’s a Sin” (2021) about young people facing the AIDS crisis in London, or “Fellow Travelers” (2023) about the Lavender Scare in the U.S., and focusing on Charleson’s dream itself rather than the injustice of what threatens it marks a distinct shift.

The broad sweep of the canvas in “La Bola Negra” heralds another major turn of the page. The play of the same name by Federico García Lorca that partly inspires the movie, and appears in one of its several timelines, is about a young man denied access to an elite social club because he’s presumed to be gay. But homophobia isn’t the primary struggle (or a harbinger of death) for the film’s other gay characters. It certainly doesn’t help two doe-eyed young men (played by Miguel Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente) brought together and kept apart by the Spanish Civil War. But the forbiddenness of their infatuation is just one current swirling around them, the most pressing of which is, well, the Spanish Civil War.

It has been revealed that weaving the fates of queer characters into the broader scope of history, and suggesting a lineage of ancestry and shared desire, as “La Bola Negra” so marvelously does, feels like a kind of imaginative reparations. And it marks a bolder, more robust tactic in humanizing queer lives; the film traces generational ties and uncovers untold histories, rather than contending with acute crises like religious doctrine or deadly disease.

There is a stranger and more expansive creative palette evidenced in these films, one that suggests the unnerving climate for queer people in the real world is only furthering the reaches of the imagination. In carrying forward the legacy of queer cinema, it seems the gays presumed buried by the trope are finally rising up.

  • It has been revealed that there's a chasm between critics and audiences that occasionally becomes wider and more noticeable.
  • This act of targeted hate designed to affect a film or show's popularity rating on an aggregator website has come to be known as review bombing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole upcoming world of cinema.

It has been revealed that there's a chasm between critics and audiences that occasionally becomes wider and more noticeable. For instance, several of Dwayne Johnson's recent movies — Red One, Black Adam, and even the Moana live-action remake — have all earned solid audience scores on Rotten Tomatoes despite having been poorly reviewed. The reverse of this phenomenon is equally prevalent. Just as a star can get their army of fans to rally behind a critically panned film, fans can also organize a mob to take down any film or show that goes against their values and beliefs.

This act of targeted hate designed to affect a film or show's popularity rating on an aggregator website has come to be known as review bombing. Typically, such campaigns are orchestrated by disgruntled fans who object to the most basic progressive ideas, such as inclusivity and diversity. This is one of the reasons why titles that have been most affected by review-bombing tend to feature actors or filmmakers from minority groups. Take, for example, Star Wars: Episode VIII — The Last Jedi, the series The Acolyte, and HBO's The Last of Us.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest examples of audiences outright rejecting a major latest project and making their dislike felt online is The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. The mega-budget streaming series recently returned with a third season on Prime Video, and while the reviews have been mostly solid, the fan reaction has been predictably unpleasant.

The Rings of Power premiered in 2022 amid reports that Prime Video invested $250 million before the show's release and committed $1 billion over five seasons. The first season of the show clocked 150 million views, according to Amazon, but reports suggested that the series struggled to retain audiences for the duration of its eight-episode run. The second season saw similar complications. The third season is getting an unusual rollout, beginning with four episodes out of the gate, with two more the next week and the final two the week after that.

It has been revealed that the Rings of Power holds an overall 83% critics' score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, but its audience score is languishing at 53%. The first season was most affected, with a 38% audience score based on more than 25,000 ratings. The third season, on the other hand, holds a 68% audience score. Viewers have been comparing the show to Peter Jackson's landmark film series, while also questioning some of the creative decisions and casting choices. You can watch The Rings of Power on Prime Video and make up your own mind. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#16383. ‘The only question is if it’s a soft recession or something more dramatic’: Gary Gensler warns the AI bubble is likely to burst and result in a recession before November 2028

‘The only question is if it’s a soft recession or something more dramatic’: Gary Gensler warns the AI bubble is likely to burst and result in a recession before November 2028

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There seems to be a slew of warning signs pointing to the inevitability of the AI bubble bursting a lot sooner than most people think.
  • In a recent development, the controversial ousting of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (who happens to be recognized as the "high priest" of the global AI buildout) and the stock market volatility tied to companies that have made huge investments in AI are two of the bigger signs pointing to the AI bubble bursting.
  • One of those individuals is the Former Securities and Exchange Commission Chair, Gary Gensler, who sat down with CNN to give his own take on the possibility of the AI burst event coming to fruition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There seems to be a slew of warning signs pointing to the inevitability of the AI bubble bursting a lot sooner than most people think.

In a recent development, the controversial ousting of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (who happens to be recognized as the "high priest" of the global AI buildout) and the stock market volatility tied to companies that have made huge investments in AI are two of the bigger signs pointing to the AI bubble bursting. Plus, there have been plenty of major personalities in the tech and business worlds who have given their thoughts on it becoming a reality at some point.

One of those individuals is the Former Securities and Exchange Commission Chair, Gary Gensler, who sat down with CNN to give his own take on the possibility of the AI burst event coming to fruition.

Here’s what he had to say and why his prediction places it near the next presidential election.

Gensler, who ran the Securities and Exchange Commission from 2021 until 2025, told CNN that today’s AI infrastructure buildout has already crossed into bubble territory and will likely lead into a recession before the next presidential election. "It's already a bubble," the former Wall Street regulator stated. "The only question is if it's a soft recession or something more dramatic.".

On the topic of all the big spending dedicated to strengthening the current AI infrastructure (which is remarked to have reached $800 billion a year by some estimates), Gensler pointed to past trends where major investments in technology eventually stagnate.

Recent findings suggest that “History tells us that when you have a upcoming technology and a significant investment ... you come to a point where it plateaus. It retrenches,” Gensler noted. “The only question is if it’s a soft recession or something more dramatic.” The previous instances he cited as massive tech investments that eventually met steep declines included railroads, 1920s electricity and the 1990s dot-com boom.

In a recent development, as for when he sees the AI bubble bursting, he points to it going down sometime before the next presidential election. "I think we're going to have this repricing and a softening of the economy that happens before November 2028," he went on to say. "I can't say exactly when and how stormy, but I would be battening down some hatches.".

Gensler is among the many other voices in the tech and investment industries who have given their thoughts on the possibilities of the AI bubble bursting and the resulting fallout. Gary Marcus, the former head of AI for Uber, argued to the Financial Times that today’s AI boom is a massive financial bubble driven by unsustainable economics and technological dead ends:.

In a recent development, “If there is a deflation of the AI bubble, the optimists say that the fresh infrastructure will remain even if the companies do not — just as railways survived the 19th-century railway bust. However, this fails to reckon with the reality of depreciation (few pieces of silicon hold their value for very long because better chips inevitably come along) and the possibility that LLMs could be displaced by more efficient models less dependent on massive numbers of expensive AI chips. In placing massive hyperscaling bets, investors are setting lavish expectations about future earnings. But LLMs are not likely to replicate the near monopolies that have made the market power of current tech giants hard to assail. A better analogy for them might be airlines, which are hobbled by small margins, intense competition, high expenses and dependence on hardware created by outside vendors.” – @garymarcus in @FinancialTimesJune 26, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the Canadian mining financier Frank Giustra was quite frank with his AI bubble burst prediction while speaking at this year’s Upcoming Orleans Investment Conference. “There will be a reckoning, and some of these companies will get destroyed," he said. During that same conversation, investor Grant Williams compared the disconnect between recognizing the stock market dangers attached to AI investments and taking proper precautions to a natural disaster.

Sources indicate that "If we told you a hurricane was heading to New Orleans, everybody would take precautions," he explained. "The interesting thing about stock market bubbles is people don't really think about what can go wrong. They're still thinking about making money.".

In a recent development, while many voices are speaking on the very real possibility of an AI bubble burst, there are business bigwigs who have made it clear that everyone shouldn’t be all that worried about it. During a sit-down interview with CNBC, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos tried to ease everyone’s fears about such a financially devastating event coming to pass. “Even if it does turn out to be a bubble, you shouldn’t worry about it because the bubble is driving investment and a lot of the investment is going to turn out to be very healthy,” he proclaimed.

It has been revealed that bret Taylor, the chairman of OpenAI and CEO of Sierra, spoke to The Verge and flat-out acknowledged that an AI bubble exists while still noting that it's totally fine. And while speaking to CNBC at the 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, his AI optimism pointed to a scenario where the market will correct itself as weaker industry players and overfunded ventures will fall by the wayside.

In a recent development, “When everyone knows that AI is going to have a huge impact on the economy across a huge range of industries and workflows, money is plentiful,” Taylor noted. “I think over the next few years, you’ll see a correction, you also see consolidation, but I don’t think you can get innovation without that kind of messy competition.”.

Gensler’s prophetic words about the AI bubble bursting before we even reach the next presidential election are alarming, yes.

But I can envision a world where potential candidates use that moment as one of their political talking points in a bid to ease back on all that AI spending, put more into the American populace and hold back on bailing out any of the AI companies that are hurting from such a traumatic event.

All signs point to something devastating happening to the AI industry at some point, especially with the huge backlash against data centers and the politicians who are looking to put in moratoriums on their continued development.

Black Friday is still a couple of weeks away, with the big shopping event falling on November 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sale is already bringing some worthwhile discounts on Soundcore's Nebula projectors. Prices start at $299 for the compact Nebula P1i and go up to $2,799 for the premium X1S 4K laser projector, with savings of up to $700 across the models we've rounded up. There's quite a bit of variety here, too, from battery-powered projectors you can take camping or move between rooms to more powerful 4K models designed for a dedicated movie-night setup.

According to recent reports, the Soundcore Nebula P1i is down to $299 from $399, while the Nebula P1 is $699.99, down from $799. Both offer 1080p resolution and Google TV, but their speaker setups are what make them interesting. The P1i has two 10W speakers that flip out and rotate to direct sound toward your seating area, while the P1's speakers detach completely and can run wirelessly for up to 20 hours. The P1 is also brighter at 650 ANSI lumens versus the P1i's 380, though you'll need a power outlet for either projector since neither has a built-in battery.

Small enough to slip into a bag, the Nebula Capsule 3 and Capsule 3 Laser are worth considering if you want something you can easily take on trips or move around the house. The standard Capsule 3 is down to $399 from $529, saving you $130, while the Laser version is $649.99, down from $749.99. Both offer 1080p resolution, automatic image adjustments, and up to 2.5 hours of battery life, although the Laser model is a little brighter at 300 ANSI lumens compared with the standard model's 200.

Taking movie night outdoors is a little easier with a battery-powered projector, and both the Nebula Mars 3 Air and Mars 3 are designed for just that. The smaller Mars 3 Air is down to $519.99 from $599.99, offering 1080p resolution, 400 ANSI lumens of brightness, and up to 2.5 hours of playback. The larger Mars 3, now $899.99 from $999.99, steps things up with 1,000 ANSI lumens, up to five hours of battery life in Eco mode, and a more powerful 40W speaker. It also has a weather-resistant design that's useful for camping or backyard screenings, though its extra bulk might make it less convenient to carry around.

If you're ready to move beyond 1080p, the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE at $1,099.99 (originally $1,299.99) offers a more affordable way to get 4K resolution. Its hybrid LED and laser light source delivers up to 1,800 ANSI lumens, while its Dolby Vision support helps bring out more detail in compatible movies and indicates. You also get Google TV and automatic image adjustments for easier setup, though it doesn't have a built-in battery, so you'll need a power outlet nearby.

At the premium end of Nebula's lineup, the X1 and newer X1S are designed for a more serious home theater setup. The X1 is down to $2,299 from $2,999, saving you $700, while the X1S is $2,799 from $3,299. Both use triple-laser technology with 4K resolution, Dolby Vision, and optical zoom, but the X1S has a considerable advantage in brightness, reaching up to 6,000 ANSI lumens compared with the X1's 3,500. That extra brightness is useful in rooms with some ambient light, but the tradeoff is louder fan noise.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. #16380. Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months.
  • Industry observers note that at long last, things are finally changing.
  • Audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Movie theater owners have been through hell.

Industry observers note that the pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months. When they could finally turn their marquees back on, Omicron and other variants made audiences skittish about returning to cinemas. Then the writers’ and actors’ strikes upended production, leaving them with fewer movies to screen. A promised moviegoing revival kept getting delayed or disrupted, often by circumstances outside of the exhibition industry’s control.

Industry observers note that at long last, things are finally changing. Domestic ticket sales are up 20 percent year over year, and with potential blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three,” “Avengers: Doomsday,” and “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” on the horizon, analysts expect revenues to easily eclipse $10 billion for the first time since COVID. Grosses in North America right now sit at $8.76 billion through November 15, fueled by franchise fare such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Toy Story 5,” but also by unconventional hits ranging from “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey” to “Obsession” and “You Can See Everything.” Related Stories Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

Audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon. And media companies, which treated the theatrical business as the sick man of the entertainment industry, are finally seeing the value in cinemas, with the likes of Amazon MGM Studios and Skydance committing to making more movies for the significant screen than most major studios did over the last decade. Better yet, younger viewers are driving the comeback, with studies showing that Gen Z members are the most frequent moviegoers.

It has been revealed that that’s the good news. Elsewhere, Hollywood seems to be crumbling. Netflix, which has done more to reshape the entertainment industry this century than arguably any other company, is teetering, having jettisoned both chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin in a brutal purge. Ted Sarandos, who is clearly feeling the heat after the company’s stock has fallen 35.6 percent year-to-date, has brought in Peter Rice, a well-regarded former Fox and Disney exec whose calm demeanor and unthreatening good looks are out of c-suite central casting, to steady the ship.

As Hollywood has stumbled around trying to develop a better business model, the solution that many companies have landed on is to get bigger, fast. Thus, Fox sold to Disney, MGM was auctioned off to Amazon, and David Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount and then promptly merged it with Warner Bros. Others, such as Comcast, spun off assets to make themselves more digestible. Has it worked? That’s the $80 billion question at Skydance, where executives have pledged to make 30 movies a year and turn a combined Paramount+ and HBOMax into a true Netflix challenger. Yet Ellison must pull this off while paying down a massive amount of debt.

It has been revealed that so far, their early moves haven’t inspired much confidence. Executives like CBS News chief Bari Weiss have embraced the Silicon Valley ethos of “move fast and break things,” but what they’ve built instead, such as a simulacrum of “60 Minutes,” doesn’t seem better than what they’ve replaced. And if, as a recent Variety story about Skydance’s post-merger strategy suggests, part of their cost savings involves making sure executives don’t send out for “sandwiches and green juices” from Erewhon, they’re in for a world of pain. They can have Jimmy John’s cater lunch, and it won’t make a dent in their debt.

Sources indicate that skydance has already laid off most of Warners’ leadership and offered buyouts to the rank-and-file. Another wave of layoffs is expected at the company any day now. And across town, those types of cuts are the default move, with everyone from Disney and NBCUniversal to Amazon and Sony slashing hundreds of jobs. Are some of these layoffs in anticipation of what a leaner, AI-assisted future might bring? Probably. But with many of these companies’ share prices flatlining or falling, they aren’t being enacted out of foresight or a position of strength.

“I can’t remember a time when things have felt so scary,” an entertainment executive confessed to me recently.

Recent findings suggest that and they’re right. It’s always popular to say the movie business is dying or the television industry is collapsing, and those doomsayers have been proven wrong time and time again. People want to be entertained. It’s just that making money entertaining them has never been harder for Hollywood.

Of course, that hasn't stopped fans from getting impatient, especially with almost three years having passed since the series first premiered. Now, with the countdown to humanity's potential extinction officially underway, we're finally getting a better idea of just how bad things are about to get.

It has been revealed that netflix has officially dropped the first teaser for 3 Body Problem Season 2. The new footage arrives just a day after Netflix confirmed that Season 2 will premiere in January on the streamer. The series has also been renewed for a third and final season, allowing David Benioff, D.B. Weiss, and Alexander Woo to complete their adaptation of Liu Cixin's bestselling trilogy.

Netflix's official synopsis for the first season reads: "Beginning during China’s Cultural Revolution in the 1960s, the series introduces a young Ye Wenjie (Zine Tseng), who makes a fateful decision that reverberates across space and time into the present day. When the laws of nature inexplicably unravel, a tight-knit group of brilliant scientists known as the Oxford Five must join forces with an unflinching detective and a mysterious intelligence agency to save the world.".

Recent findings suggest that season 2 will see humanity preparing for the San-Ti's arrival, both on Earth and in space. A fleet sets off on a mission that will take centuries to complete, while a secret hidden inside one man's mind could be humanity's best chance of surviving the invasion. And what's more, the show's creators have warned fans that if you thought Season 1 was out there, they have no idea what they're about to get themselves into, previously telling Deadline:.

“The story gets really wild in the best possible way. With something that’s that wild, there are a lot of choices to be made and a lot of things to be figured out. We’ve been putting our heads together to figure them out recently especially the past couple of months.”.

Recent findings suggest that the returning cast includes Jess Hong (Inked) as Jin Cheng, Benedict Wong (Doctor Strange) as Da Shi, Liam Cunningham (Game of Thrones) as Thomas Wade, Jovan Adepo (Watchmen) as Saul Durand, Eiza González (Baby Driver) as Auggie Salazar, and Marlo Kelly (Dare Me) as Tatiana Haas. Fresh additions include Claudia Doumit (The Boys) as Captain Van Rijn and Ellie de Lange (Wolf Hall) as Ayla, while Alfie Allen (Game of Thrones) has also joined the cast in a recurring role.

Sources indicate that 3 Body Problem Season 2 premieres January 14, 2027, exclusively on Netflix. Season 1 is available to stream now. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An upsetting revelation about Grey’s Anatomy season 23 follows its spinoff’s already discouraging delay. Returning for a record 23rd season as part of ABC’s Fall 2026 lineup, Grey’s Anatomy was supposed to be replaced by its Texas-based spinoff during midseason, as the TV series would have had to take over Grey’s Anatomy’s Thursday night timeslot. However, massive delays made such a plan unfeasible, pushing back the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff from a 2026-2027 premiere to a 2027-2028 one. ABC nevertheless revealed even more dismal news regarding the long-running medical drama.

It has been revealed that grey’s Anatomy’s third spinoff is set to be based in rural West Texas and follow doctors at a medical center in the last town for miles. Such a setting pushes the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff to be completely different from the parent series, not only for the setting, but also for the type of storylines and traumas that reach the medical center in question.

Every Grey’s Anatomy spinoff that ever existed had been filmed in Los Angeles, which prompted Shonda Rhimes and Meg Marinis’s fresh brainchild to attempt to secure a tax credit so that it could do the same. However, California refused to award Grey’s Anatomy’s spinoff a tax credit twice, resulting in the production having to be moved to Albuquerque, New Mexico.

In a recent development, this inevitably delayed production enough that the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff couldn’t debut during the 2026-2027 midseason. However, another enhancement regarding the popular medical drama is also upsetting, as Grey’s Anatomy season 23 will air its winter finale this week.

In a recent development, after airing only five episodes of Grey’s Anatomy season 23, the medical drama is set to have its winter finale on Thursday, November 19, 2026. It is the first ABC TV show to do so, accompanied only by 911: Nashville, as all the other TV series that were part of ABC’s Fall 2026 lineup are set to return after a small hiatus, before taking another one for the end-of-the-year holidays.

Grey’s Anatomy season 23 already having a winter finale date set up makes the current time particularly difficult for the medical drama, especially given that its Texas-based spinoff will be delayed for at least half a year if not more. Grey’s Anatomy season 23, episode 6’s trailer nevertheless promises an action-packed episode of medical chaos, hierarchical concerns, and personal ones too, as Richard Webber’s wish to move the patient overflow to the VIP floor seemingly puts him at odds with both Grey Sloan Memorial’s latest chief, Seth Norton, and his own wife, Catherine Fox.

While the news of Grey’s Anatomy season 23 already having a midseason finale is undoubtedly disappointing, its return has also been set up, and it’s the best possible outcome for the ABC medical drama. Unlike Grey’s Anatomy season 21, which had its midseason finale during the third week of November only to return in early March, season 23 will come back sooner.

According to recent reports, grey’s Anatomy season 23’s winter premiere is set for Thursday, January 7, 2027. This means the hiatus is only seven weeks long, which isn’t short per se, but it cannot be considered a long one either. Such a schedule mirrors Grey’s Anatomy season 22’s one from last year, when the ABC medical drama aired its midseason finale in mid-November only to return in January 2026.

Grey’s Anatomy season 23’s return schedule would have inevitably looked differently had its Texas-based spinoff begun production earlier. However, the disappointment of a longer break for the record-breaking show would have been offset by another medical drama coming from the same minds that made Grey’s Anatomy the compelling drama that it is.

With the Texas-based Grey’s Anatomy spinoff’s debut delayed, having Grey’s Anatomy return in early 2027 is the best possible news for fans of the medical drama, particularly considering how Grey’s Anatomy alternated its return date between January and March consistently in the past ten years.

It has been revealed that what started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

Industry observers note that if there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Sources indicate that here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

In a recent development, you show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

It has been revealed that I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a substantial part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

It has been revealed that blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

In a recent development, the tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a upcoming reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#16364. Breaking: Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1337 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1337 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first.
  • One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed.
  • Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

It has been revealed that the iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

Industry observers note that for years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector concern, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more notable to get a high-quality one.

It has been revealed that if you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also key to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Industry observers note that similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Industry observers note that most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

Industry observers note that one of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen indicates silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

Sources indicate that the outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

Sources indicate that however, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

According to recent reports, I won’t lie, the latest Prime Video top 10 chart isn’t all that great. But I've still been able to find three movies on the streaming service worth watching.

I’ve included a classic Christmas comedy, alongside a thrift store version of “The Odyssey," which is timely now that Nolan’s epic is finally available to watch on premium streaming this week. Oh, and the last pick is purely because of my childhood hero, The Rock. His recent Christmas caper isn’t a Rotten Tomatoes fave, but I’ll literally watch anything The Final Boss is in.

Sources indicate that the movies below are taken from Prime Video’s top 10 as of Monday, November 16, 2026. So, here are my top picks from the platform's most popular movies right now.

There’s a little-known film called “The Odyssey” that was released this year. You might have heard of it. Apparently it’s got a significant wooden horse in it… and it stars the abs of Matt Damon’s career. That gluten-free diet has made Jason Bourne look never better than in Sir Chris Nolan’s Ancient Greek tale. Oh, and there’s also 2011’s “Immortals”, which is based on similar themes that you can stream this week on Prime Video.

In a recent development, if you can’t quite fork out for Nolan’s epic this week — the standard digital edition is $19, but I couldn’t help but treat my OLED to the $29 4K Blu-ray — "Immortals” might scratch that swords-and-sandals itch. It’s not great, but it’s certainly better than 2010’s soulless “Clash of the Titans” reboot. The setup is simple: power-hungry King Hyperion (an animated Mickey Rourke) is looking for the Epirus Bow (a weapon capable of freeing the Titans). Ransacking Greece along the way, he is challenged by Theseus (Henry Cavill), leading to some visually impressive Greek spectacles.

Watch "Immortals" on Prime Video now.

In a recent development, here are the most flowers my dear old mom deserves from me. She might have exposed me to a few age-inappropriate movies back in the day — I have zero regrets and oh so much love that she let me watch “Terminator 2: Judgement Day” in 1991 when I was six years old. Newsflash: I’m old as the hills. My lovely mother’s favorite Christmas movie of all time is Will Ferrell’s classic comedy “Elf”. So it’s only polite that I rewatch it with her every Dec 25.

Recent findings suggest that the ‘favor’ part to my momma is that I have a very structured movie schedule that I absolutely watch religiously every Christmas, which makes “Elf” quite hard to squeeze in. I rewatch “The Lion King”, “Jurassic World”, “Home Alone”; and to the second at 10:35 pm, a viewing of “The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring” (Extended Version, obviously) every Christmas Day — in exactly that order. The time I have to make for the beloved festive tale of Buddy (a career-best Will Ferrell) who is accidentally stolen by Santa as a baby, raided by Elves, then eventually travels to meet his grumpy old man (the sadly deceased James Caan) after discovering his parentage is a warm-hearted, thoroughly silly treat. I know exactly why my mom loves it so much.

This week’s Prime Video top ten round-up isn’t exactly an all-timer. BUT it does include a flick with The Rock and a surprisingly jacked Santa Claus (J.K. Simmons) courtesy of a well-intentioned if not wholly successful Christmas action movie. Should we go ahead and just book The Final Boss vs. “Whiplash’s” terrifying music teacher Terence Fletcher for the main event of WrestleMania 43 right now?

Sources indicate that after Kris Kringle is kidnapped from his North Pole pad on the pesky night of Dec. 24, his go-to security guard, Callum Drift (Dwayne “The Great One” Johnson), is under a seriously time-pressed schedule to stop Christmas from being ruined. Enter Rocky’s lively co-lead, bounty hunter Jack O’Malley (Chris Evans), who isn’t exactly a fan of the holidays but begrudgingly agrees to team up to save Santa. Look, “Red One” is far from a classic — but I have so much love for my childhood hero The Rock when he was laying the smackdown in his 2000 peak — I can’t stop sticking on a guilty DJ pleasure.

Watch "Red One" on Prime Video now.
