They used Node for WebSocket connections, Erlang for the processing side, and React for a smoother frontend experience.

It has been revealed that hanna, on floor five, handles credit cards. Her team has developed a nice customer portal featuring a list of credit card charges that can be filtered and queried. Pretty charts allow you to track debt levels over time. And, for extra convenience, you can export your charges in CSV and PDF. Hannaâs team implemented all this in PHP running on Apache servers, with a frontend in Angular.

All three teams adhered to the corporate branding guidelines, so their products look and feel reasonably similar. They also work fairly well and were shipped on time.

But - great news! Megabank has hired some fresh top talent. Mike comes from the mythical lands of tech and management consultancy. Heâll be the super senior VP of platform at Megabank.

In a recent development, it takes Mike just two days to realise that work at Megabank is highly inefficient. Each team has reimplemented the same functionality over and over again. They are also relying on their own stacks, so transferring people between teams is much harder. Sure, they shipped quality products on time - but with Mikeâs process improvement expertise, imagine how much more they could be doingâ¦.

Mike creates a fourth team-the platform team. That team has two tasks:.

Soon, the platform team goes to work. They decide that backend functionality will be implemented in Go from here on, frontends in React, and everything will be hosted on Kubernetes. As far as platform teams go, this is a very modern and common-sense decision.

Recent findings suggest that the other teams start learning these technologies. Some already have some experience; others have to learn from scratch - but those are just temporary teething pains. Soon, everyone will have adjusted to the new reality and efficiency will skyrocket.

Except maybe for the investment banking team. They really need their Erlang architecture for decentralized networking - after all, they process fast-moving market data, order execution, and the like.

According to recent reports, it also turns out that Go is overkill for the credit card guys. They just need a simple model-view-controller architecture like PHP provides. Having pointers to memory addresses and managing concurrency via goroutines rather than just writing linear PHP that Apache runs in parallel is really much more than they bargained for.

In a recent development, but at least on the frontend side, a lot of time will be saved. The newly introduced list components and charts are well designed and can just be dropped into a customer portal, saving lots of development time. Except for the investment banking team - they need candlestick charts that were supported by their chart library but havenât made it into the generic charting component yet. They raise a ticket with the platform team, but it gets deprioritised since the CSV and PDF exports have to be implemented first.

It has been revealed that the credit card team is also really struggling with porting their backend to Go. They ask if they could use the transaction list from the platform team but send the same data format from their existing PHP implementation. The platform team doesnât want to be seen as the obstacle, so they agree. But writing documentation for the internal data structure of the transaction list component hasnât been planned for - after all, it was never meant to be available externally. And really, the focus right now is on building the PDF and CSV exports.

Unfortunately, this year, none of the teams will be shipping much. But Mike made an amazing presentation called âMegabank platform vision 2028 â a road to global efficiencyâ. So his bonus will be fine.

This story has played out too many times. You were probably part of it at some point. And it makes sense on its face. The inefficiencies are real. But-they are necessary. Different requirements need different solutions. Different people know different things. Standardisation and abstraction seem like good solutions on their face but are hard to implement in practice. Minor differences multiply into large, unwieldy problems.

The solution is often the opposite of what good software design teaches. Do Repeat Yourself. At least, allow for some level of repetition. But more importantly, create clear boundaries within which teams can be flexible, and clear interfaces and protocols to interact and combine their services.

This idea is as old as the internet - and is often called Service-Oriented Architecture, or SOA for short.

Think of service-oriented architecture like going to a street food market. Each vendor has a little booth with a menu of available options. If you want to order something, you know you need to talk to the vendor, request your option, and pay using a shared currency or card. Thatâs the common interface. How the vendor prepares the food, where they source their ingredients from, which kitchen appliances they use - all of that is not your concern. You interact with the common interface.

Industry observers note that for our three teams, that means that each can continue using their stack and approach and ship at their own cadence. But Mike also had a point with his platform team. There are things that are necessary for a user experience to not feel disjointed. And there are capabilities, such as DevOps, that are best handled centrally. So, rather than prescribing an exact technology stack and building shared components, Mike shifts the platform teamâs responsibility. It now:.

With these changes, efficiency rises back up. Not because the teams stopped rebuilding the same thing, but because they’ve stopped getting in each other’s way. Some code is duplicated. Some problems are solved three different ways. And that’s fine. Minimizing the amount of code written or the number of technologies used isnât a goal in itself - but building good products, shipping them on time, and allowing teams to work effectively together is. Sometimes, the most efficient thing you can do is to let people repeat themselves.

The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025.
  • “Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!).

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the Upcoming York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

It has been revealed that but even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Major Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Swiftly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

According to recent reports, it’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe massive retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Sources indicate that depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a major box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

Recent findings suggest that I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—substantial-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out promptly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

According to recent reports, yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the tech giant calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Recent findings suggest that today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word.

Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

According to recent reports, much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”.

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

In a recent development, it’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.

In a recent development, overall, this new technical post reads like Apple laying the privacy groundwork for the always-listening, always-watching products that are here and coming in the near future. It’s the privacy-first approach we’ve come to love from Apple and further demonstrates its lead on this front. I highly recommend checking it out.

OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a upcoming bar for secure payments by agents.”.

According to recent reports, chatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI states ChatGPT Wallet is the “first wallet that lets agents pay without access to customers’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”.

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users,” OpenAI explains, “so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.”.

The feature won’t work with websites that block agents, however, which has increasingly become an matter online.

Industry observers note that before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

You can read more about ChatGPT Wallet and how it works here.

The company emphasizes that payments are secure, card info isn’t shared with your dot or merchants, and that you’re in control of purchases.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we looked at how well agents used test/verification techniques in August1, we saw that GPT-5.6 Sol generally did what you might call a caricature of various techniques when asked to use a technique or library such as TDD, QuickCheck, Lean 4, etc.; not specifying any particular test method (which we'll call Default) resulted in many worthless unit tests, which was one of the best performing conditions because asking agents to test in specific ways mostly made them worse. In that eval, we gave agents the Zstd RFC and asked them to implement Zstd (with an addendum for how they should test for all conditions other than Default).

On re-running the same eval with GPT-6 Astra, we see two big differences:.

According to recent reports, on (1), we previously saw that, when implementing Zstd from the RFC with 5.6 Sol, on average, agents spent $3.50 on medium effort and $5.50 on xhigh effort to get full (holdout) test correctness about 63% and 77% of the time, respectively. With Astra, agents cost $1 to get full test correctness over 99% of the time at medium effort.

In a recent development, on (2), an example would be that when we asked 5.6 Sol to do fuzzing, it would generate many worthless random inputs, which would mostly hit the same code paths and not test anything interesting. With 6 Astra, we see agents that are asked to do fuzzing in a structured way that actually exercises code paths and finds non-trivial bugs, but we can't tell if this improved correctness or not because the Zstd implementation benchmark is saturated.

We also tried giving 5.6 Sol the IMAP RFC, but it was too hard for 5.6 Sol. When trying again with 6 Astra, we get the following distribution of results (the y-axis is the percent of runs where all tests pass; agents are not given the tests and the points are the results across 80 runs of each condition).

It has been revealed that default once again looks pretty good. Some conditions result in somewhat better correctness, but also with higher cost. Although the IMAP RFC isn't saturated, it would be nice to also see results on a harder task since most of my time goes to tasks that agents can't one-shot most of the time. To test this, we'll try the pandoc eval we looked at when comparing programming languages. A reason I want to see results on larger evals is that, as we observed when looking at caveman mode and as we saw with languages, models often perform fairly differently on larger tasks. With caveman mode, the large wins that people reported became smaller or disappeared and with languages, we saw this in multiple ways, such as C and C++ implementations of Zstd being at least somewhat ok on memory safety, whereas C and C++ implementations of Pandoc were plagued by memory safety complications.

Pandoc is significantly harder, and even after running multiple turns (roughly 14 on average), no condition reached 100% correctness, so we'll look at the fraction of tests passed instead of fraction of runs that got to 100%.

For this, we only ran each condition 25 times due to the cost involved. At MSRP, this cost about $90k.

Sources indicate that recall that, in past evals we ran on languages and test/verification techniques, the failures were often idiosyncratic results of how agents operate, such as agents using Clojure writing incorrect byte conversion code by default or agents using Verus writing vacuous proofs. This kind of thing is quite different from the reasons I've seen people say that agents should use some particular language or test/verification technique, which are generally nice-sounding explanations for why something ought to be better that sound appealing in a very human way but appear to be unrelated to reality when we look at what agents actually did2.

In a recent development, because we "only" ran $90k worth of evals here, we don't really have enough information to say why almost anything happened. We can observe that some conditions performed better than others, but it's difficult to say what it means. As a result, we shouldn't read too much into this, but we do see some things that seem consistent with what one might expect, in that we might expect most of the test techniques and libraries suggested to give better generalization, which would then give better holdout vs. test scores (result is up and to the left of the Default line when viewing visible vs. holdout test scores), with TDD giving worse generalization (down and to the right of the Default line).

But, if it's true that testing properties gives us better generalization and conditions like TDD that result in a lot of small tests give less general results, we'd expect the built-in condition to also have a low holdout:visible relative to Default and that's not what we saw. Why this is is unclear and I don't think we can really determine this without a lot more runs.

Recent findings suggest that for the actual results, the line shown for cost vs. holdout and cost vs. visible show curves fitted to the shape of all graph trajectories across multiple turns, fit to Default. Things that are below / right of the line can be thought of as worse and above / left can be considered better. With 5.6 Sol, it was clear that the test conditions generally weren't doing useful work for a combination of reasons:.

Here, we have a situation where many different techniques have a better result than Default. The conceptual error bars on each condition are quite wide (more so than indicated by the bootstrap intervals shown on the plots), but the number of conditions that outperform Default makes it plausible that one or more conditions truly outperforms Default even if we don't know which ones exactly. Furthermore, some conditions likely truly outperform other conditions, but we don't really have sufficient data to tell which conditions are generally better. It's much simpler when almost everything looks bad across a wide variety of techniques.

Here are some questions I have about the results:.

It has been revealed that if I really wanted to answer these questions, I'd want to run at least 100x what was run here to run the full matrix. Steve Yegge has mentioned using ~20 Claude subscriptions to spend ~$120k/mo of MSRP token spend. Getting to 100x isn't plausible with a setup like that, but 2x to 3x could be done with testing expanded in a limited fashion and some guesswork and extrapolation. I don't know that it really makes sense for me to do that given how much time it would take and how little spare time I have, but considering what kinds of things academics have looked at when studying programming productivity, maybe it makes sense for a grad student to do this, since it would be more informative than a number of widely cited studies. But, in industry, I'm not sure who would do this outside of an AI lab.

That being noted, if you keep in mind that we don't know how well any of these results generalize, I'll note a few things that I thought were interesting.

Industry observers note that (1): I tried to get agents to do this with the hastily written skill I wrote for the 5.6 Sol Zstd eval; although the skill performed decently, agents basically didn't do this. However, for the Pandoc eval, differential testing did cause agents to closely examine boundary conditions and figure out how to write tests (and therefore how to write code) that correctly implements both sides of the boundary. I'm not confident that this generalize, but it would be interesting to see if it does generalize and what else can get agents to do this kind of thing systematically.

(2): Although TDD underperforming is exactly what I'd expect (recall that I added TDD to the 5.6 Sol eval because I thought it would underperform), the lack of underperformance of other conditions that cause many small tests to get generated should reduce confidence in the plausible sounding reason that writing many small tests underperforms.

(3): I've felt for a long time that ACL2 is underrated relative to other verification tools (it was heavily used to good effect in industry in some areas relative to the amount of academic work on it). I had low confidence in this opinion and continue to have low confidence, but it has performed well in evals I've done so far. Given how much effort is being poured into getting agents to use Lean effectively, I'd expect that Lean will eventually outperform ACL2 even if ACL2 outperforms today, but ACL2 doesn't seem like a bad choice today. For people doing verification or proofs with Lean 4, I'd be curious how the results compare to using ACL2.

(4): Yay (perhaps). For all the reasons I noted above, I have low confidence that this generalizes, but Proptest once again performed well. And, this time, the testing was a lot better than we saw in the 5.6 Sol Zstd eval. I have no inside information on this, but I would guess that there wasn't a major effort on improving PBT / fuzzing / etc. between 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra and that this comes out of better generalization and higher capability. If that's true (and this isn't just some artifact of my only spending $90k MSRP and not $9M MSRP), this bodes well for better testing in the future in that we should expect models to get better at testing without any particular effort to improve testing capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that between my running these tests and publishing this post, a claim that you should tell agents not to write tests (based on running DeepSWE) went viral. The specific claim was.

ok it's official...[ellipses from original quote] AI-written unit tests and integration tests are empirically proven to be unhelpful. you should tell your agents to stop writing tests by themselves.

In a recent development, as we previously noted, I find DeepSWE unrepresentative of work that I do and therefore meaningless to me personally. Additionally, that was done with Sonnet 5.5 High, so it generally only passed on problems that are much easier than the problems discussed here, and as observed here and in other recent evals, which techniques are effective often doesn't generalize across problem size or problem difficulty. I find it plausible that for problems coding agents find very easy, telling them not to test reduces cost (which is what was actually shown conditional on someone caring about DeepSWE). Generalizing this to "AI-written unit tests and integration tests are empirically proven to be unhelpful" based on the test that was run seems wrong regardless of whether or not this holds for other problems, and it seems unlikely that the claim holds. The claim was based on asking for no tests, which resulted in similar correctness and a small cost savings (9%, on average). In our tests here as well as before, we find differences in correctness as well as a larger than 9% difference in cost, so it seems unlikely that a claim like "AI-written unit tests and integration tests are empirically proven to be unhelpful" based on a 9% difference in cost on a benchmark of small problems is correct. Another thing to note is that DeepSWE's grader is broken with respect to testing because (among other problems), an agent can add a test name that conflicts with a grader's secret test name, which will then cause a failure. Given issues like that, adding tests is inherently penalized in a way that isn't representative of real-world usage.

You can argue the claim was highly effective, in that making overstated claims that something is empirically proven is a good way to go viral3 or get a lot of citations, but it's not a good way to figure out how to use coding agents effectively.

In Nolan Lawson's recent post on how JavaScript framework choice impacts agents, he noted:.

My goal here is not to write the end-all-be-all benchmark for “I’m a vibe-coder, which framework should I choose?” The point of this post is to demonstrate that it’s possible in the era of AI coding to still make decisions based on evidence rather than vibes.

I feel the same way here, in that I think it's valuable to run some toy evals and see what the results are. Even if someone had the resources of an AI lab available to them, I don't think they could say that X or Y are "empirically proven to be unhelpful [or helpful]", but we can still get some kind of information.

From what we've seen in our testing evals, I'd be inclined to try proptest if I wanted a property-based testing library in Rust, and for any problem that I'd use Lean on, I'd be inclined to try ACL2 as well to see how results vary and if I get better results, and there's also a fair amount of information that fits into some kind of vibes-based feel for things.

Sources indicate that as I've noted in my N most recent posts, I've been trying to write up each of these in 30 minutes because there are too many results to write up and not enough time, so I'm not going to provide an accounting of what happened for each condition like I did for the 5.6 Sol Zstd eval. I'm already over 30 minutes on this post, so I'll stop here and perhaps we'll look more into testing and verification in a future post.

It has been revealed that thanks to Laurence Tratt, Edward Z. Yang, Sophia Wisdom, and Marco Primi for comments/corrections/discussion.

Unlike us randos, they actually have the resources to run relatively comprehensive evals and there's a general lack of information about what's effective. If people understood how to use AI better, it seems like that would result in more AI usage. Also, my experience has been that different techniques are effective with OpenAI's models vs. Anthropic's models. If one of these companies published good information about what works with their models, that could move people towards interacting with agents in a way that's advantageous for them.

According to recent reports, I guess the case against this is something like, revenue growth is so rapid that more money can be made by doing other work and/or differences in how people prompt don't really matter anyway. As someone on the outside of these labs, the former seems plausible to me, whereas the latter doesn't seem like it can be true (because I've repeatedly observed reasonable people who aren't doing obviously silly things get very different results, to the point where one person might fail to get a working solution to a problem where another person easily makes things work). To the extent the results are "real" and not an artifact of testing a broad enough set of things, the impact is larger than it might seem from just skimming the graph because, as we put more effort/turns/dollars into implementing Pandoc, we get dimishing returns with respect to correctness. This can be observed by looking at the Default fit line, which has a slope far below what we'd get if we fit a straight line from (0,0) to the Default point, as well as by looking at the curve of the fit line. Despite that, the differences I've observed w.r.t. the impact of how people prompt in practice are much larger than what we see from variying test techinque by adding a few words about how to test. I think this is fairly unsurprising (we dont really expect there to be some magic testing/verification words that give us a 10x improvement), but this kind of thing makes it difficult/expensive to run an eval that gets at differences in how people prompt.

In a recent development, btw one thing I'm noticing in my evaluations on the skill is that ChatGPT is way less into PBT than Claude is. Claude will pretty eagerly write property-based tests and seems to benefit from them during development in my current benchmarks, but ChatGPT sol doesn't do that unless you're really insistent. So there might be some prompt sensitivity going on here, or it might be model specific. I've not yet optimised the skill for ChatGPT at all so it's possible I've inadvertently fucked something up for it. BTW I don't actually know that Claude is better at PBT than ChatGPT (I should really check this). It's just more proactive about doing it, but it's plausible that when they actually write properties they're about the same level of quality.

According to recent reports, I haven't done the same breadth of testing with Claude. Given what MacIver said, it's plausible that Claude is better at property-based testing or that it's not. Also, given that he develops Hegel and is generally using Claude, it's also plausible that Hegel works better with Claude than with Codex and we'd see better results from Hegel if we tried with Claude. So there might be some prompt sensitivity going on here, or it might be model specific.

Sources indicate that although it's not shown on the graph, the original Hegel skilled used for the 5.6 Sol Zstd eval and the updated one that was created as a result of MacIver doing more testing on the skill after that eval both fared worse than Hegel with no skill. Correctness was pretty similar, and both cost a lot more, with the updated skill being the more expensive of the two. I think it's pretty interesting that this skill, which was improved for some cases got worse for other cases. As we discussed in the last post, it seems very difficult to write certain kinds of skills (such as test technique skills) that are effective across models and effort levels. A related thing we can observe here is that the Skill condition, which was a skill I swiftly whipped up based on my experience driving agentic testing with GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol outperformed in our 5.6 Sol eval, but underperformed here with 6 Astra on Pandoc. Someone who has more experience driving testing with 6 Astra on larger problems could probably write a skill that outperforms in those circumstances, at least on problems that are similar in nature to what that person has worked on, but I haven't seriously looked at Astra test effectiveness enough to write that skill myself.

Sources indicate that on a related note, for various arbitrary reasons, I've gotten used to using Codex. I seem to do ok with it. This gives me little idea how effective I would be with Claude.

Hi Dan, I was encouraged by your post about ai-coding to try fuzz/generated testing.

A part of a system I develop has a statechart-like architecture. Think of it as a support chat where automation could suggest actions or messages for support agent (human) to send to the user. LLM is not used to author messages, but just to classify some of the support intents, but state transitions are deterministic. There could also external events about the subject of the ticket that materially affect possible next actions or decisions. All of this gives rise to a rich statechart system. It is written in TypeScript.

Sources indicate that so I had to rewrite a significant chunk of that system so to derisk rewrite but also to try fuzzing I decided to go with it during the rewrite. I used sol xhigh for the first 5 days of the rewrite, then mostly astra medium or high for 4-5 days more (it was around astra release). I instructed agent to develop generate traces of all the possible kinds of events and effects that affect the logic.

Recent findings suggest that for the first 4 days it couldn't make the generated testing system find a single de novo defect that agent reviewers themselves didn't find first. I always use my approach where I define many angles/scopes/areas of review (for this rewrite there were about 15), make agents generate quite detailed prompt for these areas based on my templates, then start subagents in these areas with verbatim prompts in the areas as long as they find any defects or things to fix.

Industry observers note that in total throughout the whole rewrite, agent reviewers found about 210 bugs/defects, generated tests took off the ground a bit towards the end and produced about 20 de novo defects that agents themselves didn't notice. In total about 230.

Production code change was about 30k lines, the generated testing harness and everything that was written specifically to support this generated testing approach was about 300k lines at the end. Probably it was very ineffective, but I didn't look into it.

Sources indicate that after the deploy, there were a few (4-5) very "stupid" bugs that you would think a process that run well over 100 agent reviewers and found 230 bugs couldn't have missed. Still, I consider this a good result for a rewrite of such a complex statechart system.

Overall I consider this a negative result because generated tests helped find just 10% of the defects, and required gargantuan amount of code (300k lines) and agent tokens to develop and support.

I think this is interesting and I would love to see more people writing up case studies of what they observe.

Recent findings suggest that one I heard recently is that Rust is particularly good for agents because it has nice errors that guide agents toward the correct solution. I've seen this mentioned a few times and, while I'm not going to say this absolutely can't be true as, perhaps, a large scale set of evals that I can't really afford to run might be able to find some kind of effect, I've looked a lot harder at this than anyone who I've seen make this statement and it doesn't seem to be true for any problem that I've looked at, at least at a sample size that I can afford to run. If the statement is true, its effect seems dominated by other factors in most circumstances, so it shouldn't be a reason to choose a language; it seems like the wrong thing to mention if you're going to give a single reason Rust is a good agentic language (which is what happened when I last saw this come up).

Industry observers note that another thing to note here is that the plausible "human sounding" reasons for effectiveness are probably just as untrue when evaluating humans; it's just that we can't afford to run the human eval, so people pass around these irrefutable but also unsupported reasons. Recall that we looked at the literature on the effectiveness of static vs. dynamic types because people frequently said that studies show that static types are more effective than dynamic types, but the evidence for this claim was nearly non-existent when we looked at the major studies that had been published at the time.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Chase released a pair of statements throughout the nearly eight hour outage.
  • Tom's Guide tried to confirm with the tech giant but customers claimed that tellers at Chase locations couldn't operate their systems either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chase bank appears to be suffering an online banking outage. On the outage tracking site, Down Detector, reports slowly starting rolling in this morning before suddenly spiking around 10 am Pacific.

Chase released a pair of statements throughout the nearly eight hour outage. The bank claimed that a technical issue brought its services down and was clear that it did not consider the problems a cyberattack.

Tom's Guide tried to confirm with the tech giant but customers claimed that tellers at Chase locations couldn't operate their systems either. At least one support tweet on X seemed to confirm this.

Chase never stated if its non-digital locations were compromised.

Here's what we learned throughout the day.

@veeramarni We saw your post and want to reach out. I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking. Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience. ^RRNovember 16, 2026.

So far, I haven't seen Chase say anything on any official channels as a formal post.

The best I've come across is from Chase Support on X where the company said that it is "working to resolve an matter with online banking.".

It has been revealed that over on Down Detector reports started rolling in around 6:30 am Pacific/9:30 am ET but didn't really start spiking until 9:00 am PT. As of this posting there are more than 4,000 reports on the site.

However, if you're trying to send or receive money from or to a Chase account, you will likely have problems.

According to posters on Reddit, people have mentioned that after attempting online transactions they ended up going to their location branch.

Multiple people said that the Chase tellers told them all their systems were down and they couldn't do anything.

"Then went to branch to ask about it they noted they can’t do anything because their system is down smh," said one representative poster.

Tom's Guide has reached out to Chase for comment.

I'm seeing reports and comments that people are having trouble logging into other banks including Bank of America and Wells Fargo.

I've been able to login into Wells, but that may not be universal.

Lets u know, are you having problems with your bank?

Chase has not responded to Tom's Guide as of this posting; however, a spokesperson did give a statement to the San Francisco Chronicle.

“Due to a technical concern, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete, but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson told the paper. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”.

Analyst Bruce Schneier (Security Technologist; Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School) is an internationally renowned security technologist.

We asked him why companies don't have redundancies to prevent outages:.

"Redundancies reduce profitability, and it is the goal of shareholders these days to wring all excess profits out of any and every company. Thatreduces resilience in general, and redundancy in particular.”.

With the Outlook outage last week, and more every day, Schneier expects more will come.

"I guess I’m not surprised. Our systems are very fragile these days. Fragile systems are the most profitable in the near term. And there is no incentive to focus on the long term.”.

Reports are starting to go Down Detector, though as of this posting they are still around 4,000 after a peak of 5,000 reports about 30 minutes ago.

A Chase spokesperson has responded to our inquiries with a similar statement as the one received by the San Francisco Chronicle.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as swiftly as possible.".

However, our statement had one extra line saying that the glitch was not cyber-related, meaning it is something in the Chase systems and not a malicious attack.

"This is a technical glitch, not cyber related.”.

The spokesperson did not indicate how long it would take to resolve the issue or any potential causes.

In a recent development, yahoo! Finance is tracking statements from different banks. Wells Fargo and Bank of America have received some outage reports, but not as many as Chase, which again suggests that it's an issue between Chase and other banks.

"You can still access your accounts through our ATMs, banking locations, and customer service," the Wells Fargo website reportedly reads.

I have a Wells Fargo account and could not find that statement, but I've also had no issues logging in or using my accounts online, so my experience may not be the same.

Bank of America has not released a statement.

After an initial decline, reports on Down Detector hit a momentary plateau. For the last half an hour, they've started a slow but steady decline.

Let me know if you're able to access your Chase account since reports started going down.

As of this writing, reports are under 3,200 for the first time since 10 am PT, about 3 hours ago.

Chase has been suffering a technical outage for more than 4 and a half hours.

Again, we saw an initial stream of reports around 7 am PT/10 am ET, with the real spike hitting two hours later.

According to recent reports, chase has said in statements that the problem is a technical one, not an attack. It's not clear what the issue is and it appears to affect both online banking and in-person transactions at their banks.

In a recent development, reports have declined but not enough to declare the outage over. People are still reporting that they can't access their accounts.

We have asked Chase for clarification but haven't received any updates since the first statement.

In a recent development, I just received an update from Chase. Here's what the bank is saying now.

Per the bank's spokesperson, JPMorganChase apparently experienced a software bug in "on-premise hardware system", which the spokesperson reiterated there is "no evidence this is cyber-related.".

According to recent reports, the statement claims that customers still have access to their accounts and funds. They did not respond to questions about challenges affecting brick-and-mortar banks.

"We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today." It's unclear which timezone that end of day actually refers to.

Reports on Down Detector have halved in the last hour dropped from about 3,800 to 1,780.

Its been a slow decline but it appears things are coming back online for people.

People who've regained access have said they've been able to use Zelle, withdraw money and successfully login to the app or the browser.

For awhile it seemed reports were in steady decline, but things have remained study for the last hour.

I am seeing mixed comments from people saying they have access, while others say they still can't login to the app.

From what I can tell, the Chase outage finally appears to be over. Reports are still over 500 but most comments and social posts are indicating that people have access to their accounts again.

I have not a seen a "We're back" post from Chase or JPMorgan.

#16339. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer claims it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to substantial complications.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Industry observers note that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer claims it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to substantial complications.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Industry observers note that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Recent findings suggest that ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he claims can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

In a recent development, ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having remarked that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing firm with millions of consumers.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

It has been revealed that “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from massive data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

Sources indicate that I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and noted, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Recent findings suggest that over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Sources indicate that ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and mentioned, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one tech giant or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that indicated up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from major data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

In a recent development, when you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand newly introduced model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Industry observers note that could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Newly introduced tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

Sources indicate that one of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is crucial, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

It has been revealed that ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

According to recent reports, to make these concerns more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and claims it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

It has been revealed that ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift concern. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and upgrade the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion customers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

It has been revealed that ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s key for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

In a recent development, ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print concern as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of latest features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Industry observers note that apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a newly introduced feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:.

With Local Lists, Apple Maps users in the U.S. can find the perfect spot for meeting friends, dining, and more. Using intelligent insights from what’s trending, Maps surfaces locally relevant collections of places — from trending restaurants to great spots to take kids — so it’s easy for users to find what they are looking for. All insights are derived with privacy in mind and never tied to individual users.

It has been revealed that I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find new places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

Industry observers note that even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden.

To find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a new ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

Trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen shows only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in New York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

In a recent development, how does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”.

Yeah still not my go to navigation option. Until they can give customers the amount of information / detail / items to mark and make its alerts functioning like Waze, it won't really be much of a competitor. This stuff if great to have but why Would I want to keep switching between apps to get different information.

Maybe in 3-5 years their engineering team will mimic Waze and treat it like they've just discovered something great😒🤣.

Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple indicates you’ll want to save any places you plan to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

It’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that claims when it was last updated.

Have you used Local Lists in iOS 27’s Maps app yet? Let us know what you think via the comments.

#16336. Industry News: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays

Industry News: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cornell

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two new research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays.
  • A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed.
  • Sources indicate that “Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” said Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A solar farm in Lansing, Fresh York.

Two new research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays. One demonstrates that, in the right numbers, sheep grazing increases populations of beneficial insects like bees and lady beetles compared to mowing around solar panels. The other research describes a decision-making support tool to help farmers profitably grow their solar grazing herds.

A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed. The increase was driven primarily by an 83% increase in honey bees alone, according to the team’s findings in “Low solar-grazing densities support beneficial insects in agrivoltaic systems,” published Oct. 7 in Environmental Research Letters.

Sources indicate that “Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” said Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment. “But what’s been missing is research that treats them as parts of the same system. When we talk about sustainable solar development, integrating these discussions into a single framework is really helpful to farmers and community decision makers.”.

For three years, Zoller and a team of entomologists, ecologists and animal and plant scientists tested various stocking rates – how many sheep per hectare are allowed to graze a certain plot of land – using Cornell’s teaching sheep grazing at the university-owned Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, New York. At four sheep per hectare, they found beneficial insect abundance was similar to the mowed control site, while vegetation management effectiveness was greater than at two sheep per hectare. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation management was maximized and sheep flock health remained high, but honey bee abundance dropped by 45%.

Industry observers note that “We zeroed in on stocking rates because that’s a concrete number that sheep farmers understand and work with every day, and we want this research to be useful,” remarked Steve Grodsky, paper senior author and assistant professor of natural resources in the Ashley School. “With solar grazing, people, energy, agricultural animals, plants and insects are all part of this ecosystem. We’re trying to understand the connections between those pieces so that when solar developers, municipalities looking at solar development, or farmers are faced with a decision, they can have scientific information about potential trade-offs and synergies.”.

Grodsky is also assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey Latest York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. Additional co-authors are sheep farmer and solar grazing consultant Nikola Kochendoerfer, Ph.D. ’20; Antonio DiTommaso, professor in the School of Integrative Plant Science; John Losey, professor of entomology; Scott McArt, Ph.D. ’12, associate professor of entomology; Paige Muñiz, formerly a technician in McArt’s lab; and Todd Ugine, Ph.D. ’04, research associate in Losey’s lab, all in CALS. Sarah Carson, director of Cornell’s Campus Sustainability Office, was key in coordinating site access between researchers and the solar organization that manages the Cascadilla solar farm.

Sources indicate that another Cornell research team, from the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business, has developed a tool that helps farmers whose sheep graze in solar arrays to make better decisions about their operation. The team described the tool in “Flock Management for Solar Grazing,” which published Sept. 28 in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management.

After a chance encounter with Caleb Scott, Ithaca-based sheep farmer and founder of United Agrivoltaics, Vincent Slaugh, assistant professor at the Cornell Peter and Stephanie Nolan School of Hotel Administration and first author of the paper, began thinking through the economics and logistics of solar grazing. He recruited Linwei Xin, associate professor of operations research and information engineering, and Shane Henderson, Charles W. Lake, Jr. Professor in Productivity, both in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering, to work on the topic.

Industry observers note that together, they developed a spreadsheet-based model that helps sheep farmers to optimize procurement and sales decisions, based on factors like target flock size, costs, anticipated revenues, and expected vegetation in particular solar sites; if a farmer doesn’t have enough sheep to keep the grass down, they’ll have to cut it some other way. It also helps solar developers understand growers’ needs and develop contracts that are more profitable and sustainable for all parties long-term. United Agrivoltaics has already incorporated the tool into its onboarding process.

It has been revealed that slaugh sees opportunity for U.S. shepherds to grow their operations – especially with solar contracts offering a steady source of income and animal feed. Current domestic sheep production for meat and wool doesn’t come close to meeting domestic demand; about half of all lamb and mutton consumed in the U.S. is imported, primarily from Latest Zealand and Australia.

Sources indicate that “If we grow the sheep industry, will the American diet eventually include more lamb? Could that be a side effect of the solar energy revolution? I think the answer is very likely yes,” Slaugh remarked. “And then when that happens, we’d expect processors and supporting industries to come back, for banks to be willing to give more loans, and for supply chains to follow. All of that grows the economy, and rural economies in particular.”.

Kochendoerfer, who grazes 700 ewes on solar installations in New York and Vermont, mentioned that economy is already growing.

“I work with a lot of farms that are now scaling up because of solar,” Kochendoerfer said. “There is a newly introduced wave of sheep farmers who are capitalizing on this access to good land. With solar grazing, you get paid to graze as opposed to having to pay to graze. That leads to sustainable, meaningful economic income that these farmers can use to expand, build a barn, buy equipment or hire someone. It’s enabling a lot of folks to build sound, viable agricultural businesses.”.

Funding for these research projects came from the Cornell Atkinson Center for Sustainability, the National Institute for Food and Agriculture and the National Science Foundation.

Krisy Gashler is a writer for the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

#16335. Tech Report: The five things to look for when buying a home security camera
