Industry News: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 37 min read (7407 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~37 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing.
  • Benjamin Skuse set out to test whether AI-generated research could pass for the real thing.
  • According to recent reports, science has a spam problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing.

Benjamin Skuse set out to test whether AI-generated research could pass for the real thing.

According to recent reports, science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.

According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.

In a recent development, given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.

Industry observers note that “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”.

Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is significant—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.Round 1: Creating the ForgeryTo give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.Luigi AvantaggiatoI assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI Jorge Cuadel CalleI took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.ROUND 2: FARS1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, states Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.The AI Arms RaceOn one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.Burden on AcademicsMahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers  Round 1: The Fake PaperCreated with free versions of ChatGPT and GeminiGhost citationsMany references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.Questionable scientific claimsAn expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.Too many acronymsThe expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.Round 2: The AI-Research PaperCreated by the autonomous research system FARSToo many preprintsThe references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.Nonsense in a figureOne technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”AI artifactsAnother figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”Blurred LinesMy homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.Round 2: Using an AI Science EngineFARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.Round 2: Attempt to PublishBecause FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any challenges with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.Automation Changing the LandscapeAutomated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”Benjamin Skuse's experiment raised a bigger question: What counts as legitimate scientific research in the age of AI?Luigi AvantaggiatoIn this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future?Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud. See the AI-Generated Papers Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.

Sources indicate that the experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?

Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.

To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.

Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.

In a recent development, I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.

My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.

In a recent development, I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.

At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.

According to recent reports, what’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”.

In a recent development, other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.

I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.

For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she indicates. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”.

Recent findings suggest that though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”.

In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”.

It has been revealed that to this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he claims, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”.

Industry observers note that elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.

It has been revealed that whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud.

Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.

Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.

Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.

Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Industry News: Jiff 1.0: A datetime library for Rust

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Burntsushi

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success.
  • Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”.
  • This blog unveils the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success. Jiff automatically handles many common problems related to daylight saving time by putting time zone handling front and center into the API. Jiff has already seen widespread adoption in the Rust ecosystem.

Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”.

This blog unveils the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.

Target audience: Rust programmers who need convenient datetime handling.

In a recent development, jiff is already used in production in many projects: uv, Cargo, Starship, fd, Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and even as the basis for a Temporal implementation in AWS LLRT. It is time to call it 1.0.

Sources indicate that unless some significant defect is found in Jiff’s API, my strategy is to commit to Jiff 1.0 indefinitely. This is notable because the intent is for Jiff to be an ecosystem building block that appears in the public API of other libraries. This makes Jiff an attractive public dependency, which means semver incompatible releases are likely to cause significant pain in the ecosystem. They will not be made lightly.

To see a list of breaking changes between Jiff 0.2 and Jiff 1.0, please consult the CHANGELOG.

In a recent development, in programming, a datetime library’s core functionality rests at the intersection of a computer system’s concept of time and a human’s concept of time. The prevailing notion of system time is Unix time. A human’s concept of time is far more complex, but the most popular such model is the Gregorian calendar coupled with either a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. At the core of every datetime library rests some routine for converting between these concepts.

Industry observers note that A datetime library typically provides much more than this. Indeed, datetime handling has historically been very difficult. My own belief is that the difficulty comes from poor modeling of the domain. Instead of encapsulating the complexity inside a reusable bundle of code, many datetime libraries pass some or all of the complexity on to its people. Jiff instead tries hard to encapsulate the complexity and make it difficult for users to do something wrong. (Jiff is not the first to do this!).

In this section of the blog, we’ll do some very basic introductions.

To follow along with the examples in this blog, create a new Cargo project with dependencies on jiff and anyhow:.

According to recent reports, most examples are a complete self-contained Rust program. Just copy the code and replace whatever is in src/main.rs. Then run the program:.

Industry observers note that I am loath to present a dictionary. However, the datetime domain is littered with confusable terms, so I think it’s key to orient ourselves on a shared vocabulary. I’ve kept this section as small as possible. (Some terms, like “time zone,” are omitted here because they are best defined through exploration in the sections that follow.).

TAI and leap seconds won’t be a feature of this blog, but they are listed here in order to convey the difference between Unix time and UTC.

Sources indicate that as a way to transition into some of the core types of Jiff, I’ve come to think of its datetime types like an onion. In reverse order, we can build up its layers all the way to a ZonedDateTime. So let’s start with more terms, but this time, they are also types in Jiff:.

Recent findings suggest that to make this a bit more concrete, we can see what this looks like in code. Since a time zone can map from a civil datetime to an instant in time, one way to create a zoned datetime requires only a civil datetime and a time zone:.

Recent findings suggest that another way to create a zoned datetime requires only a timestamp and a time zone. This is because time zones can also map a timestamp to a particular civil datetime:.

Notice how we get the equivalent zoned datetime in both cases, but we come at it from different directions. In the first case, we start with a time that we might see on our clocks and calendars. In the second case, we start with a particular instant in time that we might get from a database or file system or some other system call.

There is one piece missing from the zoned datetime onion examples: the time zone offset. An offset represents the amount of time one must adjust UTC time in order to get civil time. For example, consider the time 2026-11-01T22:30:00 in UTC. In order to get the civil datetime for someone living in New York, one would subtract 5 hours:.

Indeed, every zoned datetime has an offset associated with it:.

According to recent reports, NOTE: The America/New_York string you see in the above example is an IANA Time Zone Database Identifier. The IANA Time Zone Database is a collection of time zone definitions that can be referenced by a short identifier string. Examples: Australia/Sydney, Asia/Tokyo, Europe/Berlin.

When a civil datetime is combined with an offset, then what you get is always an instant in time.

With the concept of an offset introduced, we can now give a more precise definition of a time zone. A time zone is a geographic region in which civil clocks agree and which provides the following:.

Both mappings have been demonstrated in prior examples, but the mapping from civil datetime to an offset seems to be rather complicated due to some potential ambiguity. When does that ambiguity arise? An ambiguous offset occurs when the civil datetime either doesn’t correspond to a valid clock time in this time zone (e.g., when clocks are moved ahead for daylight saving time) or where there could be multiple valid clock times (e.g., when clocks are moved backward for daylight saving time).

Let’s look at some examples. In this first example, we’ll take a look at times around the daylight saving time transition from summer time to standard time in Upcoming York. In New York, the clocks were “set back” by an hour at exactly 2AM. This caused the 1AM hour to repeat itself.

The above example highlights how Jiff resolves the ambiguity when a “fold” occurs, or when there is a time zone transition that moves the civil time backwards. But we can actually dig down into lower level APIs to change how that ambiguity is resolved. By default, Jiff uses a “compatible” strategy that always selects the first repetition of a time in a fold. But other strategies can be selected by using APIs on a TimeZone directly:.

It has been revealed that the same idea applies to gaps, or time zone transitions where there’s some civil time that gets skipped on civil clocks. For example, on March 8, 2026 at 2AM, civil time skipped ahead to 3AM:.

There are two remaining core types, both representing some notion of a duration:.

A Span is the preferred duration type to use whenever possible. Here’s a simple example that demonstrates how to get the number of days between two civil dates:.

Durations can also be added to dates:.

Generally speaking, whenever there is an operation involving a Span, there is an equivalent operation available with SignedDuration:.

Recent findings suggest that notice that in the above example, we actually switched from using a civil::Date to a civil::DateTime. This was done to show how physical time units can be added. But note that the same can be accomplished with a Span, because it combines all units:.

Industry observers note that in brief, use a Span when you can. But when it’s too bulky or too slow, use a SignedDuration. One of the key benefits of a Span is that since it represents each unit value distinctly, one can preserve the original meaning of a duration. For example, it’s common to represent the runtime of films in minutes, even when the duration exceeds one hour. Indeed, a span of 2 hours is a distinct span from a span of 120 minutes:.

Recent findings suggest that the Span::fieldwise routine converts a Span into a value whose units can be compared in a field-by-field fashion. To compare spans based on the actual physical duration they represent, use Span::compare:.

Industry observers note that this was a very brief introduction to durations in Jiff. They are a lot more powerful than what is shown here. You might even try playing with the examples above to explore its nooks and crannies. We’ll cover their API in more detail in a later section.

Jiff isn’t always the right thing to use. Sometimes you can get by with something simpler.

First and foremost, if you’re measuring the time something takes in a program, you should almost certainly be using monotonic time. This is available via std::time::Instant:.

If you do need to compute elapsed time using your system clock, then Jiff is very convenient for that:.

It has been revealed that but you don’t actually need Jiff for this. A std::time::SystemTime will work perfectly fine:.

Where Jiff starts to become useful is when you need something beyond just an integer number of seconds since the Unix epoch. For example, some very hairy math is required in order to convert a SystemTime into an RFC 3339 timestamp like 2026-11-14T21:34:00Z.

As long as you can live in UTC completely, don’t care about local time and can work with Unix timestamps only, then the Rust standard library won’t steer you wrong.

Sources indicate that conversion to and from strings is a major part of Jiff. Jiff’s focus is primarily on interoperability via the following:.

What Jiff actually implements is the Temporal RFC 9557 / ISO 8601 grammar for flexible parsing of datetimes from strings. For most use cases, it suffices to think in terms of RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601. But Jiff does support parsing strings that aren’t valid in any of those three specifications. For example, 2026-11-12[America/New_York] parses as if it was 2026-11-12T00:00:00[America/New_York].

In this section, we’ll take a tour of how Jiff does datetime formatting and printing.

In a recent development, every datetime and duration type in Jiff implements the standard library FromStr and Display traits. This means that it’s natural to parse datetimes:.

In a recent development, parsing is flexible, so even if there are components missing, parsing still succeeds. For example, without minutes or seconds, those components default to zero:.

Another example of flexible parsing is that if a string contains another date type, then one can parse that. For example, one can parse a date out of an ISO 8601 datetime:.

A ZonedDateTime always uses RFC 9557 syntax, which includes the IANA time zone identifier:.

If you want to print a zoned datetime using only RFC 3339 syntax, then you can do so by formatting the timestamp directly with the zoned datetime’s offset:.

The Span and SignedDuration types also support the FromStr and Display traits via the ISO 8601 duration format. For example:.

Since a Span is a hybrid duration that also supports calendar units, it can parse durations with calendar units and physical time units. A SignedDuration can only parse durations with physical time units:.

The ISO 8601 duration format does, however, have some shortcomings that we’ll discuss in the next section.

It has been revealed that because ISO 8601 duration strings enjoy broad support, it is the default in Jiff for both Span and SignedDuration. However, it has two important shortcomings:.

Sources indicate that the second shortcoming is best seen with an example. Consider a Span that is 2000 milliseconds. If you convert this to an ISO 8601 duration string and then parse it back, you end up with 2 seconds instead:.

This might not be desirable for cases where you want a span’s string format to faithfully represent all possible distinct values of a span.

According to recent reports, for these two reasons, Jiff comes with its own bespoke “friendly” duration format. The friendly format is non-lossy and is meant to be easier to read for English speakers than the ISO 8601 duration format. Here are some examples that are all valid friendly durations:.

Parsing a friendly duration is as easy as parsing an ISO 8601 duration: the FromStr implementations on both Span and SignedDuration support ISO 8601 durations and friendly durations simultaneously:.

Printing a friendly duration does require a bit more effort, since it isn’t the default. Instead of Span::to_string(), one can use the “alternative” syntax via Rust’s formatting machinery:.

Industry observers note that one can also use a lower level friendly printer to customize its output. For example, here’s how to write a span in the friendly format to an existing String using more spacing, longer unit labels and commas separating each unit:.

See the jiff::fmt::friendly module for a lot more detail, including a grammar that precisely specifies the format supported.

The POSIX strptime and POSIX strftime routines are far from the ideal way to format and parse datetimes, but they are ubiquitous and most programmers are familiar with them. Because of their ubiquity, and because of the utility of being able to format and parse bespoke datetime formats, Jiff provides implementations of these routines that are mostly POSIX compatible.

Every datetime type in Jiff comes with strptime and strftime routines. For example, to parse a civil date in the US month/day/year format:.

Or to format a zoned datetime in a convenient to read representation for English speakers:.

Callers can also use lower level APIs from jiff::fmt::strtime to get access to each parsed component individually:.

While the above tour should cover most use cases, there are sometimes reasons for exerting more control over parsing or formatting. Or for supporting alternate formats like RFC 2822. The jiff::fmt module is meant to cover these use cases at the cost of more complex APIs. For example, consider parsing an RFC 2822 datetime string from a &[u8] (which lets callers avoid a UTF-8 validation check):.

Another example shows how to change the default disambiguation strategy when the provided civil datetime is ambiguous. For example, Sydney, Australia moved the clocks backwards at 2026-04-05T03:00:00 local time. That is, they went from UTC offset +11 to UTC offset +10. So what happens if we try to parse a time on the clock that is repeated as a result?

Here, the first occurrence of 02:30 is selected, just before Sydney leaves daylight saving time. Now, the data itself can actually select the desired offset:.

But this happens because there is no ambiguity in the data. Since the offset is supplied, the exact instant in time is known. Going back to 2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney], which is ambiguous because it could refer to two different instants in time, how do we modify the strategy for resolving that ambiguity? We can’t using the standard library FromStr trait, so we instead have to construct our own parser manually, just like we did for RFC 2822 parsing above. This example demonstrates how to do that and all of the different disambiguation options. Remember, UTC offset +11:00 corresponds to the first occurrence of 2026-04-05T02:30 on the clocks of folks in Sydney while UTC offset +10:00 corresponds to the second occurrence.

The jiff::fmt module contains lots of other goodies that we won’t cover here, including, but not limited to:.

Industry observers note that no section on datetime formatting would be complete without addressing locales. In this context, a locale is a set of user preferences used for formatting datetimes. This is useful when you want to present a datetime to an end user that doesn’t expect standard formats from RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601.

Recent findings suggest that jiff itself does not provide any facilities for dealing with locales. Instead, customers can opt into this support via the ICU4X project. To make conversions between Jiff and ICU4X, the jiff-icu integration crate can be used.

Here’s an example showing how to format a zoned datetime in the fr-LA locale: (You’ll need to run cargo add icu jiff-icu to your project for this to work.).

In a recent development, the ICU4X API has a lot of options for customizing datetime formatting. Exploring it further is outside the scope of this blog.

Jiff provides many methods on its datetime types to make using them as comfortable and error-free as possible.

Sources indicate that every datetime type provides a fresh constructor that lets callers build it from its constituent parts. In most cases, this constructor is fallible. For example:.

Because creating dates is so common, there is a shorthand for doing so when you know the inputs are valid:.

That is, civil::date is a const function that will panic if its inputs are invalid. It should only be used with inputs that are known to be valid. It would, for example, be inappropriate to use this with user provided values. Because of the const block above, if you try to provide invalid values, you’ll get a compiler error.

For datetime types that represent an instant in time (i.e., ZonedDateTime and Timestamp), there is also a now() constructor for getting the current time:.

In addition to constructors, upcoming date values can be constructed from old date values using the Date::with API:.

Once you have a date, there are oodles of APIs available:.

Moreover, because of the datetime onion, all of these APIs are also available on civil::DateTime and ZonedDateTime:.

It has been revealed that these routines on ZonedDateTime also take time zone transitions into account. For example, ZonedDateTime knows that tomorrow() doesn’t always add 24 hours:.

NOTE: We’ll talk about date arithmetic in the next section.

When ZonedDateTime::tomorrow() (among other APIs that produce a ZonedDateTime) would land in a gap or a fold, the “compatible” disambiguation strategy is chosen automatically:.

To override this behavior, you can drop down to civil datetimes, perform the operation, and then use TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime to control the exact disambiguation strategy:.

Industry observers note that there are a few other methods of note on date types that are worth mentioning. First is the ability to query for things like, “The Thursday after next” or “The last Sunday of the month.” The former can be answered by the nth_weekday API:.

While the latter can be answered by the nth_weekday_of_month API:.

Finally, users can access a convenient time series iterator via series:.

All of these methods are also available on civil::Date and civil::DateTime, which should make it very natural to move between them.

All datetime types in Jiff support adding and subtracting durations, and finding the span of time between two datetime values. Let’s start with a civil::Date:.

Here we make use of the std::ops::Add trait implementation for civil::Date. The downside of using this, though, is that if the date value goes out of range, then it panics. That may or may not be acceptable. But if you’re dealing with user inputs, then you should use Date::checked_add instead:.

Let’s take a look at a few other examples involving months and years:.

As with other methods on Date, they are also available on ZonedDateTime:.

If we take a look at the type signature for ZonedDateTime::checked_add, we can see that it’s actually polymorphic:.

Specifically, it accepts anything that can be converted into a ZonedDateTimeArithmetic. In this case, there are From trait implementations for the following types:.

This means that ZonedDateTime::checked_add can accept any one of these duration values:.

In a recent development, this type of polymorphism is common in Jiff. Here, it is merely used to provide a convenient way to use multiple duration types. But as we’ll see, it’s also used to provide an extension point for configuration options that control how the operation works.

Industry observers note that in addition to adding or subtracting durations from datetime values, one can also compute the duration between two datetime values. For example, to get the number of days between two dates:.

Similarly, we can use Date::until to compute the span between dates:.

Like with Date::checked_add, this routine is also available at ZonedDateTime::until:.

Notice though that hours, instead of days, are returned. This is because two ZonedDateTime values might be in different time zones. Since a ZonedDateTime is fundamentally an instant in time, and because days might be of varying length depending on the time zone, defaulting to hours as the largest possible unit means subtracting two zoned datetimes will always succeed. However, we can request larger units in the duration returned by passing additional options. Notably, ZonedDateTime::until is polymorphic:.

That is, callers aren’t just limited to passing a ZonedDateTime here, but anything that can be converted to a ZonedDateTimeDifference. Here is one such example, where we can override the largest units returned in the duration:.

Industry observers note that A ZonedDateTimeDifference provides much more powerful configuration options for rounding the span returned. Take this example, which produces a span with many unit values:.

This might be too much precision to show to an end user. Instead, perhaps we’d like to round the span to the nearest half-hour. We can do this by building a ZonedDateTimeDifference explicitly and configuring its options:.

Sources indicate that note also that rounding a span takes time zone transitions like daylight saving time into account. For example, let’s take 2024-11-02 17:30 and 2024-11-03 04:45 in New York. Because New York stopped daylight saving time at 2AM on 2024-11-03, the amount of physical time between them is 12 hours and 15 minutes:.

Normally, if we rounded to the nearest day, this would round up to 1 day. But since the midpoint of this particular day is actually 12 hours and 30 minutes, this duration will round down to 0 days when we request it:.

Next we’ll continue our discussion of rounding, but when applied to datetimes themselves.

It has been revealed that date rounding in Jiff is limited to units of days or lower. Therefore, it’s only available on ZonedDateTime, Timestamp, civil::DateTime, civil::Time but not civil::Date.

A common example for rounding a datetime is to reduce precision. For example, a system clock might provide nanosecond precision, but maybe we only care about the nearest half-hour:.

As with rounding spans, rounding a ZonedDateTime is aware of time zone transitions:.

Notice that in the above example, our time of 11:45AM is before noon, yet the result still rounds up to the next day. This is because the midpoint for this day is 11:30AM since, by 11:30AM, 12.5 hours have already elapsed because of the repeated 1AM hour in the move away from daylight saving time in Fresh York.

Jiff itself doesn’t support any calendars other than the proleptic Gregorian calendar. One can instead use the ICU4X crate to work in non-Gregorian calendars, and convert between datetime types using the jiff-icu crate: (Use cargo add icu jiff-icu to make this example work.).

The ICU4X API supports many more calendars.

There are 3 potentially confusable datetime types in Jiff:.

When should you use each one versus the other?

To a first approximation, if you can use a ZonedDateTime, then that is probably the type you want to reach for. It represents a specific instant in time in a particular geographic location. That is, it has both a Timestamp and a TimeZone.

Industry observers note that if you only ever need to work in UTC or just deal with system time, then a Timestamp is probably the right choice. This is useful for representing a specific instant in time that is not connected to any time zone.

Recent findings suggest that A civil::DateTime is useful in contexts where you don’t care about a specific instant in time and when calcuations should be done independent of time zone. For example, when parsing datetime information from a user interface datetime picker.

Remember that both a civil::DateTime and a Timestamp can be converted to a ZonedDateTime by supplying a time zone.

We’ve already seen how to add spans to datetime values and how to get spans as a difference between datetime values. But we haven’t yet explored the APIs available on a Span itself.

First and foremost, we can build a Span through its constructor, which returns a Span with all of its units set to 0:.

According to recent reports, A Span is both Copy and immutable. We can create fresh spans through method chaining:.

Or we can use the ToSpan convenience trait, which adds methods on integer types for constructing spans:.

In a recent development, note though that methods like Span::hours and ToSpan::hours will panic when the integer is outside the limits of what Span supports. This is fine when your spans are literals in your program, since a panic would indicate a bug. But if your inputs come from an end user, it’s better to use fallible methods:.

Spans preserve each individual unit value. This means that 90 minutes and 1 hour 30 minutes, while they represent the same duration, are actually different values in memory:.

Sources indicate that this permits callers maximum flexibility when it comes to representing durations. This makes it possible to represent durations in a specific unit even when they add up to larger units. For example, the runtime duration of films is typically conveyed in minutes, even when the runtime exceeds one hour. This can be adjusted programmatically using Span::round:.

You can go the other way as well:.

Recent findings suggest that neither of these examples do actual rounding, despite the name of the API. Instead, since we’re only setting the largest unit, this API is doing unit balancing. Unit balancing is when all unit values rollover into larger units up until the largest configured unit. This works even for calendar units too, but you need to provide a relative date:.

Sources indicate that without a relative date, it’s not possible to know how many hours are in a single month. That is, once calendar units are involved, a span cannot be interpreted as a physical duration of time until some context is applied.

Industry observers note that the same even applies to days themselves, since days can sometimes be more or less than 24 hours. Take the above example. What happens if we use a zoned datetime as our relative date instead?

Notice that the duration’s hour component changed from 20 to 21. Why? Because we started with 2756 hour in both cases and because 2020-03-29 in Rome was only 23 hours long (in a move from standard time to daylight saving time). That means that one of those days in 3mo 23d was only 23 hours long. So an extra hour needed to be added to make up for it.

The round API can also do actual rounding:.

You can also change its rounding mode from the default (“half-expand”, or like you were taught rounding in school) to truncation (or one of several other modes):.

One can also specify a rounding increment to round to the nearest unit value. For example, to the nearest half-hour:.

Because a Span value cannot easily be compared correctly based purely on its value in memory, a dedicated comparison Span::compare routine is provided:.

In a recent development, also, one can convert a Span to a floating point value in terms of any unit. For example:.

Converting to calendar units requires a relative date for the same reasons discussed above:.

In a recent development, so far, we’ve explored a good chunk of Jiff’s API. We didn’t talk about every nook and cranny, but I think we’ve covered the most important pieces.

We’ll wrap up by briefly discussing motivation and inspiration.

Whenever I needed datetime handling in Rust, I always got confused. Should I use chrono or time? How do I get my local time from a timestamp? How do I use my system’s time zone database? How do I do calendar arithmetic?

According to recent reports, before I started working on Jiff, this confusion got annoying enough for me to consider writing my own crate. I felt like the APIs of both chrono and time could be improved upon. I personally found the domain quite interesting and so set out to build something better.

Why not improve on an existing solution, like chrono or time, instead of adding yet another choice into the ecosystem? I do think there are material downsides of having too many choices, but I had concluded that both chrono and time (in 2024) had reached a local maximum. Moreover, in 2024, I was not an expert in datetime handling. It took building a datetime library to become one. So convincing crate maintainers to go in a radically different direction would have been a tall order.

Jiff’s design and comparison documentation contain much more detail regarding the motivation and specific examples between Jiff, chrono and time.

According to recent reports, jiff is heavily inspired by Temporal, which is JavaScript’s standard library solution for date and time management. Jiff inherits API design, functionality and even parsing/formatting of datetime values. Note though that Jiff is not and does not aim to be a 100% compatible implementation of the Temporal specification. Jiff is meant to be a Rust ecosystem library first and foremost.

With that stated, if you’re familiar with Temporal and Rust, then it’s likely you’ll find Jiff to be a relatively straightforward translation of Temporal’s API to Rust. This example shows how to use Temporal to round a calendar span to the nearest number of days relative to a date:.

And here’s the equivalent operation in Jiff:.

In a recent development, the main difference between these examples is that Jiff’s duration type is named Span instead of Duration. This was done to avoid confusion with Rust’s standard library std::time::Duration type.

Here are some other differences:.

It’s easy to say that without Temporal, Jiff wouldn’t exist in its current form today.

10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason.
  • In a recent development, the story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast.
  • Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering newly introduced depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

In a recent development, the story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

It has been revealed that if Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae indicates up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

It has been revealed that looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

According to recent reports, love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

In a recent development, if you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Industry observers note that emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

Industry News: Epic formally asks SCOTUS to uphold contempt ruling against Apple

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions.
  • As most 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple and Epic Games have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle since 2020, when Epic sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store.
  • The move came after Epic remotely activated an alternative payment system that bypassed Apple’s In-App Purchase system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Here are the details.

As most 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple and Epic Games have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle since 2020, when Epic sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store.

The move came after Epic remotely activated an alternative payment system that bypassed Apple’s In-App Purchase system.

Although the court largely sided with Apple, it did rule that the company could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple ultimately allowed those links, but imposed new restrictions, including a 27% commission on external purchases, in addition to new rules limiting how developers could display buttons and links to alternative payment methods.

Epic challenged those restrictions, and the court agreed that Apple had violated the original injunction, holding the tech giant in civil contempt.

Apple has since attempted multiple times to overturn that ruling, arguing that the original injunction contained no explicit prohibition on imposing those restrictions.

Epic, on the other hand, argues that Apple deliberately circumvented the court order by introducing upcoming rules designed to achieve the same result as those originally prohibited.

Sources indicate that in May, Apple appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to hear the case. Apple submitted its opening brief in September, followed by supporting briefs from the U.S. government and several legal and business groups.

Those included the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Chamber of Progress, and several former federal antitrust enforcers. In a nutshell, the U.S. government argued that the original injunction did not clearly prohibit Apple’s 27% commission on external purchases, but maintained that the organization was correctly held in contempt for restricting how developers could display external payment buttons.

Today, Epic filed its official response.

In its opening brief, Apple argues, citing multiple legal precedents, that courts must enforce the letter of an injunction rather than its broader spirit.

According to the company, there was nothing in the original injunction explicitly prohibiting it from charging commissions on external purchases or imposing additional restrictions on payment links, so it should not be held in contempt for conduct that the court order did not clearly prohibit.

In its response filed today, Epic disputes Apple’s interpretation of the injunction, arguing that the company “attempts to avoid contempt by proposing an extreme legal standard.”.

[Apple] argues that a court can find contempt only if an injunction spells out the exact practice at issue–so an injunction barring Apple’s then-existing anti-steering rules left it free to implement new ones that prevent steering just as effectively. Nothing in this Court’s precedents supports that approach, which would reduce injunctions to a never-ending game of whack-a-mole.

Epic argues that “Apple devised a plan to circumvent the injunction,” claiming that “Apple chose a rate of 27% for the commission, knowing that, when combined with the developers’ payment-handling costs (more than 3%), the rate for linked-out purchases would be higher than the rate for purchases using Apple’s payment system.”.

As an Apple executive admitted, every “linked-out transaction is going to be more expensive to any developer * * * than an IAP transaction at 30 percent.” Apple simultaneously commissioned a “sham” report to try to provide an economic justification for the commission; the report contained an “entirely manufactured” rationale for the 27% rate.

The organization also argues that “Apple tried to cover up its scheme to circumvent the injunction” by asserting privilege over more than 57,000 documents, and points to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers’ finding that “its Vice President of Finance ‘outright lied under oath’ when he testified about when Apple decided to impose the latest commission.”.

Finally, Epic asks the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling against Apple or, if the justices decide to clarify the legal standard for contempt, to send the case back to the lower courts for reconsideration under that standard.

With Epic’s response now filed, Apple has until December 14 to submit its final brief before oral arguments take place on January 11, 2027.

Recent findings suggest that stephen Wilson Jr. is having a great Monday.

Alongside the Grammy news that his offering “Gary” is up for Best Country Solo Performance and “Hardwired” for Best Country Song, Wilson declared his sophomore double album Impressiøn of a Human // Children of the Cørnerman, which is slated to arrive Feb. 26, 2027. The ambitious LP will follow his 2023 Bon Aqua EP, which featured the searing “American Gothic” and “Year to Be Young 1994,” and Wilson’s colossal 22-track debut album, Søn of Dad. The double album announcement also dropped alongside the rollout of Wilson’s single “I’m a Song,” a stunning duet with Chris Stapleton that the two will perform at the CMA Awards on Wednesday.

The song, which was penned years ago and previously released as a live recording, was a favorite of Wilson’s father, Stephen Wilson Sr., who died at 59 in 2018 and has inspired much of Wilson’s work. When discussing the origins of “I’m a Song” on Theo Von’s podcast, Wilson described how his father watched him perform it live for the first time at Bluebird Cafe in Nashville, capturing his performance on his giant cellphone. A month later, on Father’s Day weekend, his father told Wilson that was his favorite song of all time. “He was actually my first fan. He believed in me so much more than I ever believed in myself,” remarked Wilson. Sources indicate that over the weekend, Wilson performed “Wonderwall” for Oasis at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony.
